definition.title: What are cycling power zones?
definition.answer: Cycling power zones are watt ranges built from your FTP. Each range gives a structured workout a repeatable intensity target, from easy recovery riding to short anaerobic efforts.
definition.detail: This page uses the Coggan 7-zone model as the cycling default. Friel stays under cycling; Vance and Stryd are labeled as running-power models so the same zone number is not mistaken for the same intensity.

limits.title: How to read these zones
limits.description: Power zones are practical training bands, not measured physiological borders.
items: A stale FTP or CP shifts every zone, so update the reference after a reliable retest.
One watt at a boundary does not change the purpose of a workout; follow the full interval and how it feels.
Zone 7 is an open-ended neuromuscular range. A percentage of FTP cannot predict personal sprint power.
Power meters, smart trainers, and running-power devices can read differently. Keep the device and calibration context with the result.

coggan.title: Coggan 7 zones at 250 W
coggan.description: With an FTP of 250 W, see how recovery, endurance, and harder efforts translate into watts.
coggan.caption: Coggan power zones at 250 W
coggan.note: At 250 W, Coggan zone 2 is 138–188 W and Friel zone 2 is 140–189 W. This tool gives every whole watt one zone: a rounded Coggan upper edge stays in the lower row, and the next watt starts the next row. Small boundary differences are display rules, not physiological thresholds.
coggan.source: Reference: Andrew Coggan’s power training levels. This table retains this tool’s whole-watt conventions; the top two zones are simplified guides, not predictions of sprint capacity.

models.title: Which model to use
models.description: Use the model named in your training plan. A zone number can represent a different intensity in another model.

cards.coggan: Default cycling model. Seven zones from the published Coggan edges: under 55%, 56–75%, 76–90%, 91–105%, 106–120%, 121–150%, and above 150%.
cards.friel: The same classic 7 names, with non-overlapping watts. At 250 W, endurance (Z2) is 140–189 W (56–75%), and zone 1 is 139 W or below.
cards.vance: A running-power 7-zone set: recovery through anaerobic capacity, with narrower middle zones than Coggan. Use it with the reference your running plan uses.
cards.stryd: A 5-zone running model, usually anchored to CP: easy, moderate, threshold, interval, and repetition.

faq.question: What is Friel zone 2 at 250 W?
faq.answer:
At 250 W, Friel zone 2 (Endurance) is 140–189 W, or 56%–75% of the reference. Zone 1 is 139 W or below. This page assigns the shared boundary to the higher zone, so Friel ranges do not overlap.

Use this range with a cycling plan based on the same model. Near a boundary, follow the purpose of the whole training segment instead of chasing a 1 W change.

faq.question: What are Coggan zones at 250 W?
faq.answer:
Coggan’s 7 zones at 250 W are Z1 under 138 W, Z2 138–188 W, Z3 189–225 W, Z4 226–263 W, Z5 264–300 W, Z6 301–375 W, and Z7 above 375 W. Zone 2 is still based on the published 56–75% band. The displayed whole-watt ranges are continuous: a rounded upper edge stays in the lower zone, and the next watt starts the next zone.

These are intensity references, not seven workouts to complete every day. Find the zone in your plan and consider your readiness for that session.

faq.question: Is Friel the same as Coggan?
faq.answer:
No. Both are classic 7-zone cycling models with the same names: active recovery, endurance, tempo, threshold, VO2max, anaerobic, and neuromuscular. Their percentages and boundary rules differ. On this page, Coggan keeps a rounded upper edge in the lower zone, while Friel assigns a shared calculated boundary to the higher zone. At 250 W, Coggan Z2 is 138–188 W and Friel Z2 is 140–189 W.

This describes the implementation in this tool. When comparing platforms, check the model version, percentages, and rounding convention together.

faq.question: What is a power zones calculator?
faq.answer:
A power zones calculator turns a known cycling FTP or CP into training ranges in watts. Enter the reference, pick Coggan, Friel, Vance, or Stryd, and copy the table for endurance and intervals.

The scorecard keeps your reference, model, and watt ranges together. Share links restore the same inputs for a discussion with your coach or training partner.

faq.question: Should I enter FTP or CP?
faq.answer:
Enter the reference you already train with. Cyclists usually enter FTP. Runners with power often enter CP. This page does not decide which one is “correct.” It only scales the selected model from that number.

FTP and CP are different metrics. Switching the label does not convert the value, and a cycling reference should not be transferred directly to running.

faq.question: I don't have an FTP or CP yet. Where do I start?
faq.answer:
Use the FTP calculator for a 20-minute, ramp, 2×8, or 60-minute test, or the critical power calculator for two or three hard efforts. Bring that number back here.

A reference you already train with is enough. At 250 W, Coggan endurance (Z2) is 138–188 W. Update the watts when you retest.

faq.question: Why can zone edges differ by 1 W?
faq.answer:
Whole-watt ranges need an explicit rounding rule. For Coggan, this page keeps a rounded upper edge in the lower zone and starts the next zone one watt later, so every watt has one home. Friel, Vance, and Stryd assign their shared calculated boundary to the higher zone.

A 1 W difference between platforms is usually a display convention, not a change in fitness. Compare the model, percentages, and rounding rule before changing a workout target.

faq.question: When should I use Vance or Stryd?
faq.answer:
Use them for running with power, not as a substitute Coggan cycling chart. Vance is 7 zones with narrower tempo and threshold cuts. Stryd is 5 zones and is usually anchored to CP. If your bike plan says Coggan or Friel, stay on those.

Even if two models both use Z3, follow each model’s percentages and training guidance. Keep your device, reference, and plan consistent when comparing sessions.

faq.question: Do power zones map directly to heart-rate zones?
faq.answer:
There is no direct one-to-one mapping. Power describes external output at that moment, while heart rate also changes with duration, conditions, and your physical state.

When a plan specifies power, follow its power targets and use heart rate and perceived effort as additional context. Two zones named Z2 need not represent the same intensity.

faq.question: Should I recalculate after changing devices or updating FTP?
faq.answer:
Recalculate when your FTP or CP changes. Keep a record of the reference and model used at the time when comparing past sessions.

After changing power devices, check how each measures power and compare readings. Cycling watts and running watts are not interchangeable training targets.

faq.question: Can I print or share this scorecard?
faq.answer:
Print keeps the colored scorecard on one landscape page. Share copies a link that restores the same watts and model. A result is saved in Trainingload.ai only when you choose to keep it there.

This page uses the watts you type. Ride files stay on the FTP and critical power calculators, where they are read in the browser and are not uploaded.

formula.title: How are the watt ranges calculated?
formula.equation: Zone boundary (W) = power reference × zone percentage
formula.body: For a 250 W FTP, 55% is 137.5 W and 75% is 187.5 W. This tool rounds those edges to 138 W and 188 W, so Coggan Z2 is shown as 138–188 W. Each whole watt belongs to one zone. Changing the model changes the boundaries; selecting FTP or CP changes the reference label, not the metric itself.

methods.title: Methods and formulas
methods.description: Multiply average power by time to get work, then fit a work–time line. Its slope is CP; its intercept is W′.
methods.caption: Critical power methods

rows.bestFor: A shorter and a longer record for an initial estimate
rows.limit: Two points define a line; fit cannot be assessed

rows.bestFor: An extra record to assess agreement with the model
rows.limit: A good fit does not validate maximal capacity

methods.example: Example: 3 minutes at 400 W + 12 minutes at 300 W → CP 266.7 W, W′ 24.0 kJ. The scorecard rounds CP to 267 W.

details.title: Two-point calculation
details.formula: CP = (P₂t₂ − P₁t₁) / (t₂ − t₁); W′ = P₁t₁ − CP × t₁
details.method: Convert average power (W) × time (s) into work (J), then find the line through the two points.
details.basis: The slope is CP and the y-intercept is W′.
details.limits: Durations must differ and both CP and W′ must be positive. Similar durations amplify input errors.

details.title: Three-point fit
details.method: Convert three records to work, then fit a work–time line using least squares.
details.basis: R² is calculated on work; the largest residual is expressed in watts for comparison with the inputs.
details.limits: A high R² only describes closeness to the line. Consider power residuals, effort intensity, and measurement conditions too.

details.title: Power estimates by duration
details.method: Insert a duration into the same model to estimate average power.
details.basis: Calculations use unrounded CP and W′; the card displays whole watts.
details.limits: These are model predictions. Fatigue, environment, fueling, and pacing affect actual performance.

faq.question: What is critical power?
faq.answer:
Critical power (CP) describes sustained power and a boundary in how the body responds to exercise intensity. Expressed in watts, it is estimated from performance at different durations and can help guide training.

Below CP, physiological responses such as oxygen uptake can stabilize under suitable conditions. Above CP, that stability cannot be maintained and exercise tolerance is limited. Adding 20 W when you are well below CP therefore has a different significance from adding 20 W when you are already above it.

CP is not defined as your average power for a fixed 30 or 60 minutes, and it does not mean power you can hold indefinitely. In the chart, CP is the horizontal line the power curve approaches. This calculator estimates it from your records; subsequent rides help you interpret the result.

faq.question: What is W′?
faq.answer:
W′, pronounced “W prime,” is the finite work available above CP in the two-parameter model. It is measured in joules or kilojoules. CP is a power; W′ is an amount of work. They describe different aspects of performance.

For example, with CP of 250 W and W′ of 20 kJ, riding at 350 W uses 100 W above CP. The model gives 20,000 J ÷ 100 W = 200 seconds, or about 3 minutes 20 seconds. This illustrates one continuous high-intensity effort; it does not guarantee that performance on a particular day.

Two riders with the same CP but different W′ may perform differently on a climb or acceleration lasting several minutes. W′ helps explain that difference, but it is not peak sprint power or a literal anaerobic battery. Aerobic and anaerobic energy contributions do not switch on and off at CP.

faq.question: How is CP different from FTP?
faq.answer:
CP fits power records across multiple durations and also estimates W′. FTP is a threshold-power metric commonly used in cycling, usually estimated from a specific test or activity data. Both can guide training, but their definitions and methods differ. Similar values are not proof that they are interchangeable.

Our FTP calculator has two paths. Manual test power is converted using the selected test method. File estimates first fit CP from extracted power records, then estimate FTP as CP × 0.95 under the current implementation. That factor is a product estimate, not a universally accurate physiological conversion.

This scorecard displays CP, and the linked power-zone calculator uses CP as its reference. If an existing plan is based on FTP, check which metric it expects before changing it. CP adds information through W′, but using a CP model does not automatically make every estimate more accurate.

faq.question: Can I use regular ride records?
faq.answer:
Yes. You can start with regular rides instead of completing a dedicated maximal test first. At least two different durations with valid average powers can produce an estimate when fitted CP and W′ are positive. File estimates can also use power segments from an existing ride.

What changes is how representative the result is. Easy or deliberately restrained segments describe the relationship between those records, but may say less about your maximal capacity. Unequal restraint in the short and long records can move CP either up or down, so the result is not automatically a lower bound.

Compare it with your previous setting, recent workout completion, and perceived effort before deciding whether to adopt it. Recalculate when you have more representative records. A targeted test can improve confidence; it is not a prerequisite for obtaining an estimate.

faq.question: How long should the efforts be?
faq.answer:
Choose clearly different durations, such as 3 and 12 minutes. A 6-minute record can add a useful middle point. Manual inputs accept 2–30 minutes, with roughly 3–20 minutes a reasonable starting range. This is guidance for selecting data, not a rule that prevents other accepted durations from being calculated.

Enter average power over the entire selected segment. A 12-minute input needs that segment’s 12-minute average, not peak power, whole-ride average, or Normalized Power (NP). The duration and power must describe the same segment.

A 3-minute and a 3½-minute record can be calculated, but their small separation makes the fit sensitive to measurement differences. Recent records with comparable fitness, power meters, and recording methods are easier to interpret. They do not have to come from the same day.

faq.question: How do file estimates work, and what data do I need?
faq.answer:
File estimates read the ride’s power time series and find the best average power over the selected durations. You can choose 3 + 9 minutes or 3 + 30 minutes. Those two records feed the CP and W′ calculation, scorecard, and chart. Whole-ride average power is not treated as CP.

The activity must be long enough and contain readable timestamps and power. A power meter, smart trainer, or another power-recording device can supply this data. GPS position, speed, or heart rate alone cannot fit this model. A FIT, TCX, or GPX extension does not guarantee that power is included.

The best segments may overlap within the same ride, so they are not equivalent to two independent maximal tests. Use Enter power to inspect or edit the extracted values. If power is reported missing despite being recorded, check export options and try the device’s original FIT file.

faq.question: How do two records produce CP and W′?
faq.answer:
First multiply average power by duration to obtain work. Watts multiplied by seconds give joules. For 3 minutes at 400 W, work is 400 × 180 = 72,000 J. For 12 minutes at 300 W, it is 300 × 720 = 216,000 J.

Plot those points against time. The line’s slope is CP: (216,000 − 72,000) ÷ (720 − 180) ≈ 266.7 W. Subtract CP × time from the first record’s work to get W′ = 24,000 J, or 24.0 kJ. The scorecard rounds CP to 267 W.

Power curve and Fitting process are two views of this same model: P = CP + W′ ÷ t, and work = CP × t + W′. Switching views does not change the algorithm. With three records, least squares finds the work–time line that best fits the three points together.

faq.question: What do a third record and R² add?
faq.answer:
Two distinct durations always determine a line, so the two-record result says Two-point solution rather than R² = 1. A third record lets you check whether another duration agrees with the relationship. The fit adjusts both CP and W′ to bring the work–time line close to all three points.

Add 6 minutes at 350 W to the 3-minute 400 W and 12-minute 300 W example. CP becomes about 264 W, W′ becomes 27.0 kJ, and R² is about 0.998. Yet the largest power residual is still about 14 W. A high R² does not mean every duration is predicted closely.

R² is calculated on work against time; the largest residual is converted to watts for comparison with the records. These describe model fit, not an accuracy percentage. Neither proves the power meter was error-free or that all records reflect maximal capacity.

faq.question: How should I use the 5-, 8-, and 20-minute estimates?
faq.answer:
These values use P(t) = CP + W′ ÷ t. The calculator converts duration to seconds, uses unrounded CP and W′, then displays whole watts. They are modeled sustained powers, not three additional personal bests found in your file.

For the 3-minute 400 W and 12-minute 300 W example, estimates are about 347 W for 5 minutes, 317 W for 8 minutes, and 287 W for 20 minutes. They can help you compare the demands of shorter climbs, longer accelerations, and sustained efforts against your actual records.

Interpret predictions more carefully as they move beyond the durations you entered. Predicting 20 minutes from 3- and 9-minute records is extrapolation. Modeled 20-minute power is not FTP, and these numbers are not targets you should ride to exhaustion in every session.

faq.question: How can CP and W′ guide training and pacing?
faq.answer:
Use CP as a power reference, then choose intensity around the purpose of the session. Endurance riding, work near threshold, and shorter high-intensity efforts involve different combinations of power and duration. This page can switch zone models and carry CP into the power-zone calculator. Switching models changes zone boundaries, not your CP.

W′ can help explain why repeated accelerations affect the latter part of a ride. Work above CP draws on the model’s finite work capacity, while recovery at lower power takes time. A hard start well above CP on a long climb may therefore make the second half harder to sustain. Use this to compare pacing ideas alongside terrain and perceived effort.

This page does not track remaining W′ throughout an activity or simulate recovery intervals. Interval planning still needs duration, repetitions, recovery intensity, and actual completion. The estimate is an input to planning, not a complete training plan.

faq.question: How is power-to-weight calculated, and what does it tell me?
faq.answer:
Power-to-weight is CP divided by body weight, in W/kg. This page uses the rounded CP on the scorecard: 267 W ÷ 70 kg = 3.81 W/kg. Weight only affects this ratio. CP, W′, and the curve can be calculated without it; switching metric and imperial units converts the weight.

The ratio helps compare power across body sizes, but absolute power still matters. At 4 W/kg, a 60 kg rider produces 240 W and an 80 kg rider produces 320 W. Equal ratios do not imply equal flat-road speed, aerodynamic drag, or short-duration acceleration.

Because the numerator here is CP, an FTP classification table does not directly apply. For progress comparisons, look at CP, body weight, and comparable input records together. A rise in W/kg caused solely by a weight change does not necessarily mean sustained power has increased.

faq.question: Why do different calculators give different CP values?
faq.answer:
Inputs may differ first. One tool may use best segments from a single ride, another may use best records across several weeks, and another may use two or three manual points. Durations, pause handling, missing power, and rounding can all affect results.

Fitting methods also differ. This page uses a two-parameter work–time model. Even when tools show P = CP + W′ ÷ t, minimizing errors in work versus power can produce different answers. Some tools use a third parameter to change the short-duration curve. More complexity is not a guarantee of greater reliability with limited data.

Compare the records and model before comparing the numbers. For long-term tracking, keep the calculation method and record selection reasonably consistent. A higher CP immediately after changing models first indicates changed calculation conditions, not necessarily improved fitness.

faq.question: What are the limits of this calculator?
faq.answer:
This is a simplified model that summarizes a few power records as CP and W′. It does not separately model peak sprint power, fueling on long rides, heat, accumulated fatigue, or riding position. Avoid using the same curve to predict both a few seconds of sprinting and several hours of riding. Meter errors, missing samples, and mismatched segments also affect the result.

Compare estimates with recent performance. Repeated sessions that feel much easier or harder than expected, old input records, or a change of meter or indoor/outdoor conditions can justify recalculating. There is no mandatory update schedule, and one poor day does not require an immediate change.

Review the new result alongside the old value, input records, and completed training. You decide whether to adopt it. Calculating or sharing this scorecard does not automatically change your personal training settings.

faq.question: What is lactate threshold?
faq.answer: Lactate threshold is the highest intensity you can sustain before fatigue accumulates quickly. In training it is a practical marker for heart rate, power, and pace—not a lab blood-lactate curve. This calculator estimates that field-test proxy so you can set zones and compare trends.

faq.question: How do I estimate or determine lactate threshold from a field test?
faq.answer: Pick a recent race for threshold pace, or use a repeatable field test: a 20-minute effort for LTHR, a 20-, 8-, or 60-minute test for threshold power, or a hard time-trial whose pace is already the threshold effort. The primary result is labeled LT2, with an LT1 band beside it.

faq.question: How is LTHR different from max heart rate?
faq.answer: LTHR is the heart rate at sustainable threshold (LT2). Max heart rate is the peak from a short all-out effort. They are not interchangeable, and LTHR is not a fixed percent of HRmax. Many athletes land somewhere around 80–90%, but the spread is wide enough that a formula from age or from HRmax is only a rough start. Use a max heart rate calculator when you need HRmax. Use a steady 20-minute average, or the last 20 minutes of a 30-minute time trial, when you need LTHR.

faq.question: How does this relate to FTP?
faq.answer: FTP is a common cycling name for threshold power. This page estimates that field-test proxy from a timed effort (20-min × 95%, 8-min × 90%, or 60-min). It does not analyze an uploaded activity file. If you want FTP from a GPX, FIT, or TCX file, use the FTP calculator.

faq.question: How accurate is a field-test lactate threshold estimate?
faq.answer: A field test or a race-derived pace estimates lactate threshold. It is not a lab blood-lactate measurement, and the LT1 band is a percentage of that LT2 estimate, not a mmol/L curve. Accuracy depends on pacing, freshness, protocol, and conditions.

faq.question: What is the difference between LT1 and LT2?
faq.answer: LT2 is the higher threshold: the intensity where fatigue rises quickly and a hard effort lasts closer to 20–60 minutes. LT1 is the lower aerobic threshold, where the effort is still sustainable and you can usually speak in sentences. This page estimates LT2 from a race or a field test, then shows LT1 as a percentage of that estimate: about 81–89% of LTHR, 70–80% of threshold power, or 82–90% of LT2 speed. Those bands match the zones this site already uses. They are not a measured lactate curve in mmol/L.

faq.question: How does threshold pace compare with tempo pace and half-marathon pace?
faq.answer: Threshold pace on this page is LT2, often called T-pace: a comfortably hard effort you might hold for about 20–40 minutes in a workout. Tempo usually sits a notch easier, around the top of the LT1 band or in the gap between LT1 and LT2, so it is easier to repeat inside a week. Half-marathon pace is often close to LT2, especially around 1:20–1:45, because that race is long enough to sit near threshold. A 5K is clearly faster than LT2, and a marathon is clearly slower. Use the chart or the race calculator instead of treating those names as one pace.

faq.question: How does a watch lactate-threshold estimate compare with a race-derived one?
faq.answer: A watch lactate-threshold test, including a Garmin guided test, estimates LTHR and sometimes pace from a ramp or a detected deflection. It is convenient and repeatable on that device, and it depends on the strap or optical sensor, the protocol, and the model in the firmware. A race-derived pace uses a finish time you already have and the same threshold-band model as this calculator. When the two disagree, prefer the one that matches a recent, evenly paced effort in the sport you are training, then retest. Averaging a watch number with a race number does not make either one a lab lactate test.

faq.question: Which race distance is the best input?
faq.answer: A 10K or a half marathon is usually the closest single race to threshold duration, so the conversion to LT2 is smaller. A 5K is shorter and more anaerobic, so LT2 pace comes out slower than 5K pace and leans more on the model. A marathon is much longer, so LT2 pace comes out faster than marathon pace, and heat, fueling, and a late fade move the finish time. Use the most recent race you paced evenly. If you already have a threshold time trial, enter it as a threshold effort rather than as a race.

faq.question: What is lactate threshold?
faq.answer:
Lactate thresholds describe changes in the blood-lactate response as exercise intensity increases. Definitions depend on the test and interpretation method, so threshold is not one universal heart rate or a fixed 20- or 60-minute average.

For everyday training, threshold heart rate, power, and pace are useful working references. This page estimates them from records; it does not read blood samples or produce your personal lactate-concentration curve.

faq.question: How do LT1 and LT2 differ, and are both measured here?
faq.answer:
LT1 usually describes a lower lactate transition; LT2 refers to a higher intensity boundary. Neither should automatically be equated with the boundaries of every five- or seven-zone training system.

The main result comes from performance conversion or a selected heart-rate, power, or pace record. The LT1 reference is a separate heuristic: roughly 81–89% of LTHR, 70–80% of threshold power, or 82–90% of threshold speed.

For example, 172 bpm gives 139–154 bpm, and 247 W gives 173–198 W. These ranges are starting references, not evidence that your individual LT1 lies inside them.

faq.question: Can I use an ordinary run, a 7K, or a 10K?
faq.answer:
Yes. Run result accepts matching distance and time, including a custom distance. Segment pace directly uses the selected segment’s average. You do not need to complete an all-out 5K before calculating.

Interpretation still depends on the record. Reserved effort, terrain, heat, or an easy session can change how well it represents current ability. Compare the estimate with previous references and recent training, then decide whether to adopt it.

faq.question: Should I use Run result or Segment pace?
faq.answer:
Run result converts distance and time into effective VDOT, then takes the T-pace midpoint. A 20:00 5K has an average pace of 4:00 /km; the model estimates threshold near 4:22 /km, or 7:02 /mi. It does not add a fixed number of seconds.

Segment pace simply divides time by distance. Use it for a segment you consider representative of threshold. The two paths may produce different results from the same input because they answer different questions.

faq.question: Why use the last 20 minutes of a 30-minute heart-rate effort?
faq.answer:
Joe Friel’s common field method uses the average heart rate from the last 20 minutes of a 30-minute time trial after warming up. Sampling later reduces the influence of heart rate catching up at the start.

Manual mode accepts your selected average. File mode computes a time-weighted mean over the final 20 minutes. Ordinary records can be processed too, but a segment that was not near threshold remains a reference for that effort rather than a validated LTHR.

faq.question: What happens when I use an activity file?
faq.answer:
The file is read in your browser, without uploading it. FIT, TCX, and GPX availability depends on the timestamps and sensors inside, not just the extension. You can choose start and end times.

Heart rate uses the last 20 minutes; power uses the first 20-minute average times 0.95; pace uses distance and elapsed time. Heart rate and power need at least 95% time coverage, without filling gaps longer than 10 seconds.

Pauses count toward elapsed time, and zero power counts toward the average. Extracted numbers remain visible under Enter values. A shared link contains calculation values, not your activity file.

faq.question: Are threshold power, FTP, and CP the same?
faq.answer:
This page uses FTP-style field estimates: 20-minute power ×0.95, the mean of two 8-minute average powers ×0.90, or a direct 60-minute average. For example, 260 W ×0.95 gives 247 W.

CP is fitted from multiple durations and is accompanied by W′. FTP, CP, and laboratory LT2 have different definitions and should not be treated as interchangeable. File mode here uses 20-minute power; the FTP calculator’s file mode fits CP, so those paths can return different estimates.

faq.question: Is the relative-intensity reference a training-zone model?
faq.answer:
Heart-rate and pace modes place your estimate beside a heuristic LT1 range to explain relative intensity. This is not a newly defined five-zone training system. Faster pace has a smaller time value, unlike increasing heart rate or power.

For training zones, pass LTHR to the heart-rate zone tool. Power mode offers Coggan, Friel, Vance, and Stryd: changing models changes boundaries, not the FTP estimate. Follow the model used by your sport and training plan.

faq.question: Why does my watch give a different threshold?
faq.answer:
Compare the inputs and method first. A watch may combine continuous sensor data and activity history; this page uses the record you select. Equipment, route, weather, and fatigue can also change the result.

Look for consistency with repeatable recent performance rather than simply averaging two estimates. Check heart-rate records for dropouts, optical errors, or drift. Without blood-lactate sampling, both results remain estimates.

faq.question: Does a higher LTHR mean better fitness?
faq.answer:
Not by itself. Heart rate varies with the person, sport, conditions, and fatigue. A higher LTHR does not automatically mean better endurance or a higher maximum heart rate.

More useful comparisons include pace or power at a similar heart rate under similar conditions, and how the same output feels. Keep running and cycling references tied to records from their respective sports.

faq.question: How should I train with the result?
faq.answer:
A threshold is a reference for planning intensity, not a target for every session. Easy work, continuous efforts, and intervals serve different purposes; duration, recovery, and repetitions matter too.

The examples insert only the metric you calculated. Pace does not produce an invented personal heart rate or power. Start with manageable work and compare breathing, form, sensor response, and recovery.

faq.question: When should I recalculate, and does this update my settings?
faq.answer:
Recalculate when recent performance repeatedly differs from the old estimate, when better records become available, or when equipment and conditions change. There is no need to test on a fixed schedule or change threshold after one poor day.

Keep the old inputs and method for a meaningful comparison. Calculating, printing, or sharing this scorecard does not automatically update personal training settings; adopting the result is your decision.

tempo.title: Steady tempo
tempo.body: Run 20–40 minutes continuous at {pace}. If you train by heart rate, stay near {hr}. On the bike, hold about {power}. Keep it even. This should feel like LT2, not like a 5K.

cruise.title: Cruise intervals
cruise.body: Run 4–6 × 1 km at {pace}, with 60–90 seconds of easy jogging. Heart rate can settle near {hr} on the later reps. On the bike, the same idea is 4–6 × 4 minutes at {power}. The short rest lets you practice threshold without one long grind.

progression.title: Progression
progression.body: Run 30–40 minutes from the LT1 band ({lt1Pace}, or about {lt1Hr}) and finish the last 8–10 minutes at {pace} / {hr}. On the bike, start near {lt1Power} and finish near {power}. Arrive at LT2. Do not start there.

aerobic.title: Between LT1 and LT2
aerobic.body: Run 30–50 minutes slower than {pace}, from about {lt1Pace} up toward threshold, or from {lt1Hr} up to just below {hr}. On the bike, stay around {lt1Power} to just under {power}. Use this when a full LT2 session is too much for the week.

pace.tempo: After warming up, run near {value} for a controlled continuous block, initially 10–20 minutes. Extend it only when breathing and form remain manageable.
pace.cruise: Try 3–4 blocks of 5 minutes with 1–2 minutes of easy jogging. Use {value} as a reference and aim for consistent completion.
pace.progression: Start easy and gradually approach {value} later. The {easy} range is a heuristic, not a number you must force yourself to hit.
pace.aerobic: Keep easy training comfortable. Check the {easy} reference against conversation and recovery rather than pushing every run toward {value}.

heartRate.tempo: Once settled, observe heart rate near {value} during a threshold block. Heart rate lags: do not accelerate sharply just to reach the number.
heartRate.cruise: Split the work into shorter blocks and compare later heart rate with {value}, alongside pace, breathing, and form.
heartRate.progression: Warm up easily and increase gradually. {easy} is a ratio-based reference; {value} is your estimate, not a replacement for how the effort feels.
heartRate.aerobic: Start with comfortable breathing and conversation, then check {easy}. Heat or fatigue can raise heart rate at the same pace.

power.tempo: After warming up, complete a manageable block near {value}. Start with 10 minutes and adjust duration based on how it goes.
power.cruise: For example, try 3 × 6 minutes with 3 minutes of easy riding, using {value} as a reference. Keep form and output consistent.
power.progression: Start at an easy output and approach {value} later. {easy} is a heuristic range, not a mandatory starting point.
power.aerobic: Compare {easy} with how easy riding feels. A zone model organizes intensity; it does not require you to raise a recovery ride’s average power.

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have resting HR and HRmax, Karvonen (HRR) is a good default. If you have a reliable LTHR estimate, Friel can be more actionable. If you only know HRmax, use the Max HR model.

faq.name: Why do my zone boundaries differ by 1 bpm?

acceptedAnswer.text: This tool rounds bpm values and assigns boundaries to the higher zone so output ranges do not overlap, which can create a 1 bpm difference.

answer.description: Use heart-rate zones to turn a known benchmark into practical training targets.
answer.body: Heart-rate zones split HRmax, heart-rate reserve, or LTHR into practical intensity ranges. They help you separate recovery, aerobic, tempo, threshold, VO2max, and anaerobic work using the heart-rate benchmark you actually know.

cards.friel: Uses lactate-threshold heart rate (LTHR) to build a more detailed seven-zone structure.
cards.mhr: Uses percentages of max heart rate (MHR) to build five zones when that is the only benchmark you know.

faq.question: Can I estimate zones from an ordinary workout?
faq.answer:
Yes, if the recording contains enough steady, hard work. A complete 55-minute ride with a steady 30-minute section can produce an activity-based LTHR estimate and an observed peak heart rate.

A finishing surge does not prove your threshold is higher, and the observed peak is not the same as a physiological maximum.

faq.question: Does the activity file leave my browser?
faq.answer:
The file is read in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

A FIT, GPX, or TCX stays on this device while the estimate is calculated.

This page does not store the file or write the estimate into an account.

faq.question: Why do these zones differ from my watch?
faq.answer:
Watches often use another percent table. Friel's running bands start Zone 2 higher than the cycling table used here.

The same LTHR can show a different Zone 2 on a running profile.

This page keeps the cycling and general table so Zone 2 matches the Zone 2 calculator.

faq.question: How do I train with these zones?
faq.answer:
Use the zone that matches the session you planned.

A long endurance day stays in the aerobic zone instead of drifting into tempo.

The range is a target for that session, not a guarantee of a particular adaptation.

faq.question: What are the limits of a one-activity estimate?
faq.answer:
One qualifying activity is enough to produce an estimate, but the result only describes that recording.

An easy day may return a lower LTHR estimate than a value you already trust. That alone does not mean your threshold has declined.

faq.question: Will this page save my zones?
faq.answer:
This page does not save results or replace a value you already use.

Print the scorecard or share the link when you want to keep the numbers.

Replace the example result with your own values before you treat it as yours.

faq.question: Which model should I use?
faq.answer:
Use the model that matches the benchmark you already have: heart-rate reserve, LTHR, or max heart rate.

If you know resting heart rate and max heart rate, Karvonen uses both.

Switching models changes the table. It does not change the measurement you entered.

faq.question: Where do I get max heart rate or a Zone 2 range?
faq.answer:
Max heart rate formulas live on the max heart rate calculator. A Zone 2-only range lives on the Zone 2 calculator.

Estimate HRmax there, then bring the number back here for the full table.

This page shows every zone for the model you select. It does not replace those two tools.

methods.title: How the zones are calculated
methods.body: Karvonen zones use heart-rate reserve: resting heart rate plus the reserve times the band. Friel zones use the cycling and general LTHR table, with Zone 1 under 81% and Zone 2 from 81% through 89%. Friel's running table starts Zone 2 higher, and this page does not use it, so Zone 2 stays aligned with the Zone 2 calculator. Max-HR zones apply the same five bands to maximum heart rate. Each bpm edge is rounded once, and the next zone starts one beat later.

faq.question: How do I convert GPX, FIT, or TCX files?
faq.answer:
Choose the target format, upload one GPX, FIT or TCX file, then convert and save the download. One file is processed at a time.

You can also use a specific direction page below, such as FIT to GPX. They use the same conversion service.

faq.question: Which conversion directions are available?
faq.answer: This hub covers GPX, FIT, and TCX in both directions: FIT to GPX, GPX to FIT, TCX to GPX, GPX to TCX, FIT to TCX, and TCX to FIT.

faq.question: What are the file limits?
faq.answer: One file at a time, up to 16 MB. GPX, FIT, and TCX only. KML and KMZ are not supported.

faq.question: What data is preserved or lost?
faq.answer: The converter keeps the GPS track and common activity fields when they exist, such as time, elevation, heart rate, cadence, and power. Device-specific or developer fields may be dropped if the target format cannot store them.

faq.question: Is my file uploaded?
faq.answer: Yes. The file is uploaded so the converter can create your download. This public tool does not save the file to a Trainingload.ai account. Do not upload files that contain information you do not want to send.

faq.question: Is this a free GPX FIT TCX converter?
faq.answer: Yes. You can convert endurance activity files online and download the result with no install.

faq.question: Can I convert KML or KMZ to GPX here?
faq.answer: No. This converter accepts GPX, FIT, and TCX only. Export the route to GPX in Google Earth or your mapping tool first, then convert that GPX here if you need FIT or TCX.

faq.question: How does a FIT Course differ from a FIT activity?
faq.answer:
A Course is intended for route navigation; an activity records a completed session. Both can end in .fit, but their contents serve different purposes.

Use this tool to prepare a route for navigation. To change the format of a completed activity, use the GPX, FIT and TCX activity converter.

faq.question: Which source files can I use?
faq.answer: Choose one GPX, TCX or FIT file containing a GPS route or track. An indoor session with heart rate or power but no coordinates cannot supply a navigation route.

faq.question: Will the result work on my device?
faq.answer:
Your device or platform must support FIT Course imports. After downloading, use its import process and check the start, finish, direction and completeness before heading out.

Navigation features vary by device. Converting formats does not add route planning or guarantee turn instructions.

faq.question: Does it change my original file?
faq.answer: No. The converter creates a new download and leaves the original file on your device unchanged. Keep the original so you can check the result or export it again.

faq.question: Is the file uploaded?
faq.answer:
Yes. The file is sent to the conversion service to create the FIT Course download. Using this public converter does not automatically add it to your training account.

For local inspection of FIT contents, use the FIT file viewer.

faq.question: Why did conversion fail or produce an incomplete route?
faq.answer:
Check that the source includes coordinates, opens normally and was exported completely. Format conversion cannot restore missing or damaged records.

Try exporting again from the source platform and checking the format. Keep the error details if you need help investigating.

metadata.title: Privacy Policy | Trainingload.ai
metadata.description: How Trainingload.ai collects, uses, shares, retains, and protects account, training, health, location, and AI data.

openGraph.title: Privacy Policy | Trainingload.ai
openGraph.description: Understand what data Trainingload.ai uses and the choices you have.

overview.title: Privacy at a glance
overview.body: Trainingload.ai helps you understand training load, review completed workouts, and manage training plans. Some features need health, fitness, or location data. We treat that information as sensitive and design the Service around data minimization, clear choices, and user control.
items: We do not sell personal data and do not use health, fitness, location, or AI conversation data for third-party advertising.
Connecting fitness platforms, syncing HealthKit, using precise location, and enabling AI features are optional and controlled separately.
You can export eligible data, disconnect providers, withdraw AI permission, delete Coach conversations and activities, or delete your account.

scope.title: 1. Who we are and what this policy covers
scope.body: Trainingload.ai is operated by the developer identified on the app store or distribution channel through which you obtained the Service ("Trainingload.ai", "we", "our", or "us"). This Policy applies to our mobile apps, website, web app, Apple Watch experience, APIs, support, and related services. "Personal data" means information that identifies you or can reasonably be linked to you. This Policy does not replace the privacy notices of services you choose to connect.

dataWeCollect.title: 2. Data we collect
dataWeCollect.body: The data we collect depends on the features you choose to use. It may include:
items: Account and profile data: name, email address, profile image, language, time zone, account identifiers, sign-in provider identifiers, and a securely hashed password when password sign-in is used.

Training and activity data: workout type, date and time, duration, distance, route and GPS coordinates, elevation, pace, speed, heart rate, power, cadence, calories, laps, training load, performance estimates, perceived exertion, and imported or generated workout files.

Health, wellness, and body data: data you enter or authorize from HealthKit or connected services, such as body mass, resting heart rate, heart-rate variability where available, sleep, steps, active energy, recovery trends, VO2max, thresholds, zones, goals, competitions, and plan history.
Content and communications: Coach prompts, voice transcripts you choose to submit, AI responses, reviews and plans, notes, support messages, feedback, and files you upload.

Connection and transaction data: connected-provider account IDs, authorization tokens, granted scopes, sync settings and status, product and subscription status, purchase and transaction identifiers, and billing support records. We do not receive or store your full payment-card number.

Device, location, and usage data: IP address, device and browser type, operating system, app version, language, time zone, cookie or local-storage identifiers, screens and features used, access times, crash and diagnostic metadata, and precise location when you permit route recording.

sources.title: 3. Where data comes from
sources.body: We collect personal data from the following sources:
items: Directly from you when you create an account, complete your profile, upload a file, record a workout, write or dictate a Coach message, configure a plan, make a purchase, or contact support.

From your device when you grant access to HealthKit, location, microphone, speech recognition, or other operating-system capabilities. Apple Speech Recognition may process microphone audio to produce a transcript; Trainingload.ai sends the transcript only after you choose to submit it and does not store the raw Coach recording.
From services you connect, including Apple, Google, GitHub, Garmin, COROS, Intervals.icu, Strava, Polar, Wahoo, and Suunto, according to the permissions and sync directions you select.
Automatically through essential service logs and, when enabled, privacy-limited analytics and diagnostics.

howWeUse.title: 4. How we use data
howWeUse.body: We use personal data only for the purposes described below:
items: Create and secure your account, authenticate you, remember settings, and provide support.
Import, record, store, export, and synchronize workouts and health data at your direction.
Calculate training load, zones, trends, performance estimates, recovery context, and plan-versus-completed comparisons.
Provide training plans, Coach conversations, activity reviews, and user-confirmed plan adjustments.
Process subscriptions and purchases, restore entitlements, send service messages, and maintain transaction records.
Detect abuse, investigate errors, protect the Service, and improve reliability and product quality using minimized, aggregated, or de-identified data where practical.

connectedServices.title: 5. HealthKit, location, and connected services
connectedServices.body: These integrations are optional. We request access when you choose the related feature and use the data only within the scope described to you.
items: HealthKit: the iOS app may request read access to workouts and workout routes, heart rate, resting heart rate, active energy, steps, walking/running and cycling distance, running speed, and running stride length. Authorized samples and derived summaries may sync to your Trainingload.ai account so they are available across your devices.

Precise location: the mobile app uses location to record outdoor routes, measure distance, and perform pre-start checks. For activity weather, we may send Apple WeatherKit the activity's approximate midpoint coordinate and time rather than the complete route.

Fitness platforms: depending on the provider and your settings, we may import or export activities, planned workouts, wellness summaries, sport settings, and the identifiers needed to maintain synchronization.

Authentication and connection credentials are used to sign you in or perform the synchronization you requested. We request the minimum practical scopes and do not use imported fitness data for advertising profiles.

You may revoke device permission in system settings or disconnect a provider in Trainingload.ai. This stops new collection or synchronization from that source, but does not automatically delete data already imported into your account.
connectedServices.note: HealthKit data is used for health and fitness functionality and is not used for advertising, data brokerage, or sale. Trainingload.ai is not a healthcare provider, and the Service is not a medical device.

ai.title: 6. AI Coach and third-party AI
ai.body: AI features are optional. Before any AI request is sent, the app presents a separate disclosure and asks for your explicit permission.
items: Recipient: AI requests are sent to DeepSeek, operated by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd. DeepSeek states that data it receives may be processed and stored in mainland China.

Data sent: your submitted prompt or speech transcript and only the training context relevant to the requested feature. This may include sport, duration, distance and elevation derived from a route, aggregate heart-rate and zone data, pace, power, cadence, load, recovery trends, goals, plans, and relevant profile settings.

Data not attached by Trainingload.ai: your name, email address, account ID, complete GPS track, and raw HealthKit samples. Your own prompt can still contain identifying or sensitive information, so do not include information that is unnecessary for the request.

Purpose and provider use: data is sent to generate the Coach reply, plan, adjustment, or review you request. DeepSeek's current public terms state that, after secure encryption and strict irreversible de-identification, it may use inputs and outputs to a minimal extent to provide, maintain, operate, develop, or improve its services. We do not claim that DeepSeek provides zero retention or zero training.

Storage: Trainingload.ai stores submitted prompts, transcripts, generated replies, plans, and reviews in your account to provide the feature and history. Coach conversations remain until you delete the conversation or account; reviews and plans remain with the related record until that record or account is deleted, subject to legal retention requirements.

Control: you may decline AI and continue using non-AI features. You can withdraw permission in Mobile Me > Privacy & AI or Web Account Settings > Privacy & AI; this blocks new AI requests and automated reviews but does not delete existing results. A provider or material disclosure change requires permission again.

Safeguards and limits: requests use encrypted transport, direct account identifiers are removed from generated training context, and AI content is not copied to a separate AI observability provider. AI output can be inaccurate and is for informational and training-support purposes, not diagnosis or medical advice.
ai.note: For a provider-side deletion request concerning an AI request, contact support@trainingload.ai. We will assess and route applicable requests according to the provider's process and applicable law.

sharing.title: 7. When we share data
sharing.body: We share personal data only as needed for the Service, when you direct us to, or when law requires it. Recipients may include:
items: Infrastructure and storage providers, including Cloudflare R2 when configured, and database, cache, hosting, content-delivery, and security providers that operate the Service.

Authentication and connected-service providers, including Apple, Google, GitHub, Garmin, COROS, Intervals.icu, Strava, Polar, Wahoo, and Suunto, when you sign in, connect, import, export, or disconnect.

Billing providers, including Apple and RevenueCat for App Store purchases and supported web billing providers such as Creem or Waffo. They receive account, product, subscription, and transaction information needed to process and reconcile purchases.

Analytics and reliability providers, including PostHog, Google Analytics, and Sentry when enabled. We configure these services to limit collection and do not intentionally send workout content, precise routes, HealthKit samples, or AI prompts and responses as analytics events.

Apple WeatherKit for activity weather context, Apple Speech Recognition for optional dictation, email delivery providers for account and support messages, and DeepSeek for AI requests after permission.

Professional advisers, authorities, or other parties when reasonably necessary to comply with law, protect rights and safety, investigate abuse, resolve disputes, or complete a merger, financing, acquisition, or sale of assets subject to appropriate protections.
sharing.note: We do not sell personal data. We do not share health, fitness, location, or AI conversation data with data brokers or unrelated third parties for their advertising. We require and confirm that processors receiving user data provide the same or equivalent protection described in this Policy and required by applicable law; if that protection cannot be maintained, we will stop the affected transfer.

analytics.title: 8. Cookies, analytics, and diagnostics
analytics.body: Our website and apps use local storage, cookies, and limited analytics or diagnostics to operate and understand the Service.
items: Essential storage keeps you signed in, remembers settings, protects sessions, and supports requested functionality.
PostHog and Google Analytics may receive events such as page or screen views, feature interactions, app version, platform, locale, time zone, and an account or device identifier when enabled.

Mobile analytics disables session replay and automatic remote feature collection, disables IP-based geolocation in PostHog, and filters property names associated with prompts, messages, precise coordinates, health metrics, activity IDs, and similar sensitive content.
Sentry may receive crash, request, device, network, and user or session metadata needed to diagnose failures on affected web properties. AI prompt and response content is not intentionally included.

You can use browser, device, and available in-product controls to limit non-essential storage or analytics. Where applicable law requires opt-in consent, non-essential technologies should be activated only after that consent.

retention.title: 9. How long we keep data
retention.body: We keep personal data only as long as reasonably necessary for the purpose collected, taking account of the data's nature, sensitivity, legal requirements, and whether the purpose can be achieved another way.
items: Account, profile, training, HealthKit, location, plan, and imported data generally remain while your account is active or until you delete the relevant item.
Coach conversations remain until you delete the conversation or account. Withdrawing AI permission stops new transfers but does not automatically erase existing conversations, plans, or reviews.

Temporary local processing copies used during cloud-object-storage uploads are scheduled for deletion after 24 hours; retained source files and derived records otherwise follow the related activity or account.

An in-app account deletion request blocks account access immediately. Automated deletion normally completes within 24 hours and may take up to 7 days. Connected credentials are revoked or cleared, stored files are deleted, and account-linked database records are purged.

We may retain limited transaction, fraud-prevention, security, dispute, or legal records for the period required by law or reasonably necessary to establish or defend legal claims. Where practical, these records are separated from the deleted account and pseudonymized or de-identified.

security.title: 10. How we protect data
security.body: We use technical and organizational measures designed to protect personal data. No system can guarantee absolute security.
items: Encrypted transport for network requests and restricted access to production systems.
Data minimization, permission scoping, deletion workflows, and separation of public and private storage.
Secure password hashing and protection of authentication and integration credentials appropriate to their use.
Monitoring, rate limits, audit records, and incident investigation procedures intended to detect abuse and operational failures.

transfers.title: 11. International processing and transfers
transfers.body: Trainingload.ai is offered globally, and we and our providers may process data outside your country. Privacy laws in those locations may differ from those where you live.
items: Depending on deployment and provider settings, infrastructure, analytics, diagnostics, billing, and connected-service data may be processed in the United States and other countries where those providers operate.
DeepSeek states that AI request data may be processed and stored in mainland China. This location is disclosed again before you enable AI.

Where applicable law requires it, we use recognized safeguards for international transfers, such as contractual protections, data minimization, encryption, and transfer assessments, and honor applicable rights regarding those transfers.

legalBasis.title: 12. Legal bases for processing
legalBasis.body: Where laws such as the GDPR or UK GDPR apply, our legal bases depend on the feature and purpose:
items: Contract: to create your account and deliver the training, synchronization, support, and billing functions you request.

Consent: for optional permissions and processing such as connected-provider access, HealthKit, precise location, microphone and speech recognition, third-party AI sharing, and non-essential analytics where required.
Legitimate interests: to secure, debug, and improve the Service, prevent abuse, and understand minimized usage patterns, after balancing those interests against your rights.
Legal obligation and legal claims: to comply with tax, accounting, consumer-protection, law-enforcement, and other valid legal requirements or to establish, exercise, or defend claims.

rights.title: 13. Your choices and privacy rights
rights.body: Depending on where you live, you may have some or all of the following rights. We may need to verify your identity before completing a request.
items: Access personal data we hold about you and obtain information about how it is used and shared.
Correct inaccurate account or profile data.
Export eligible account and activity data in a portable format.
Delete an activity, Coach conversation, connected service, or your account, subject to limited legal exceptions.

Withdraw consent, object to or restrict certain processing, and opt out of sale, targeted advertising, or qualifying profiling. We do not sell personal data or use it for decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
Complain to your local data-protection authority. You will not be discriminated against for exercising a privacy right.

children.title: 14. Children's privacy
children.body: The Service is not directed to children under 13 or a higher minimum age required by local law, and we do not knowingly collect their personal data without valid authorization. If you believe a child has provided data improperly, contact us and we will investigate and delete it where appropriate.

updates.title: 15. Changes to this policy
updates.body: We may update this Policy when our product, providers, or legal obligations change. We will update the date above and provide additional notice or request renewed permission when a change is material and applicable law or platform rules require it.

notices.title: 16. Third-party notices
notices.body: The providers below control their own services and publish separate privacy notices. Their policies apply when you interact directly with them. Our responsibility for processors acting on our instructions remains subject to applicable law and our agreements.

contact.title: 17. Contact us
contact.bodyPrefix: For privacy questions, rights requests, or complaints, contact
contact.bodySuffix: . Please include your account email and the request type, but do not send passwords, authentication tokens, raw health files, or other unnecessary sensitive information by email.

faq.question: What is FTP (Functional Threshold Power)?
faq.answer:
FTP, functional threshold power, is the cycling power you can hold for about an hour. It is a training anchor. Once you have it, interval length and intensity can be written as a percent of that number.

The plain definition is the highest power you can sustain for 60 minutes. Field tests shorten that. A 20-minute effort is common because a full hour is hard to pace. On this page that shortcut is the 20-minute average × 0.95. A real 60-minute average is FTP with no extra factor. A ramp uses the last completed minute × 0.75. Two 8-minute efforts use their average × 0.90.

The number is only useful if you can repeat the effort that produced it. Use it to set zones and to compare a later test done the same way. It is a field estimate, not a laboratory lactate curve.

faq.question: What is a good FTP?
faq.answer:
Watts move with body mass, so a watt figure is a rough reading until you divide by kilograms. The Allen and Coggan table on this page turns the men's W/kg cuts into example watts at 65, 70, and 75 kg. Those watt columns are not targets for the women's column.

At 70 kg the men's cuts are: untrained under 156 W, fair 156–195 W, good 195–274 W, excellent 275–353 W, and superior 354 W and above. At 65 kg the same cuts are under 145 W, 145–181 W, 181–255 W, 255–328 W, and 328 W and above. At 75 kg they are under 167 W, 167–209 W, 209–294 W, 295–378 W, and 379 W and above.

A newer rider is often in the fair-to-good span. At these weights that is roughly 150–250 W. Superior starts at 354 W at 70 kg, so a result in the mid-300s is already the top published category. This page does not add a separate elite band above that. The cuts are rounded, and a result within a few hundredths of a line is the same practical category.

faq.question: What is a good power-to-weight ratio?
faq.answer:
Power-to-weight is FTP in watts divided by body mass in kilograms, written W/kg. It is the fairer comparison when riders are different sizes, and climbing speed follows it more closely than watts alone.

The result card uses four round bands, the same for every rider. Under 2.5 W/kg is Recreational. From 2.5 up to but not including 3.5 is Club. From 3.5 up to but not including 4.5 is Strong club. 4.5 W/kg and above is Competitive. A rider who trains regularly is often in Club. Strong club, 3.5 to under 4.5 W/kg, is where many competitive amateurs sit. These four bands are not race categories, and they are not split by age or sex.

The Allen and Coggan table further down uses different cuts for men and women, from Untrained through Superior. Men: untrained under 2.23, fair 2.23–2.78, good 2.79–3.92, excellent 3.93–5.04, superior 5.05 and above. Women: untrained under 1.90, fair 1.90–2.35, good 2.36–3.32, excellent 3.33–4.29, superior 4.30 and above. There is no band above Superior on this page.

faq.question: How do FTP power zones work?
faq.answer:
A zone is a percent of the FTP on the card, so the same effort is repeatable. This page uses Allen and Coggan's seven zones. Z1 Active recovery is below 55% of FTP. Z2 Endurance is 56–75%. Z3 Tempo is 76–90%. Z4 Threshold is 91–105%. Z5 VO2max is 106–120%. Z6 Anaerobic capacity is 121–150%. Z7 Neuromuscular is above 150%.

At a 250 W FTP, tempo (Z3, 76–90%) is 189–225 W, and threshold (Z4, 91–105%) is 226–263 W. This site displays continuous whole-watt ranges: the rounded upper edge stays in the lower zone, and the next watt starts the next zone. Some plans call about 88–94% of FTP a sweet spot. On this split, 88–90% is still the top of Tempo and 91–94% is the bottom of Threshold. The table does not add an eighth zone.

Open power zones on the card when you want Friel, Vance, or Stryd boundaries from the same FTP. Those models use different cuts. Repeat the same test before you move the targets.

faq.question: What is the difference between typing a test and uploading a ride file?
faq.answer:
Typing is the main path, and it does not need a file. Enter the average power of the cycling effort you rode. A 20-minute average is multiplied by 0.95, so 250 W becomes 238 W. A ramp uses the last completed one-minute step × 0.75, so 320 W becomes 240 W. Two 8-minute efforts use their average × 0.90, so 270 W becomes 243 W. A 60-minute average is FTP with no factor: 240 W for the hour is 240 W FTP.

The ride-file tab is a separate cycling estimate. Upload one GPX, FIT, or TCX file containing power data. A 30-minute time trial uses the best 30-minute power and the best 3-minute power. A 3/9 test uses the best 9-minute power and the best 3-minute power. Those two points are fit to critical power, and FTP is that critical power × 0.95, rounded. Ramp (×0.75) and 2×8 (×0.90) are not applied to a file.

The share card and the copied link use the protocol, power, and weight you type on the field-test tab. The shared URL stores weight in kilograms.

faq.question: How do I read the result card?
faq.answer:
The large number is FTP in watts. The line under it repeats the formula. For a 20-minute test, 250 W × 0.95 = 238 W. For an hour, the line shows that 60-minute average equal to FTP.

Add body weight to see W/kg and one of the four bands. At 238 W and 70 kg, W/kg is 3.40, which is Club: 2.5 up to but not including 3.5. Without weight, the card still shows FTP and the seven zones, and it asks for weight before it shows a band.

The zone table is the seven Coggan percents of that FTP. Print keeps the card. Copy link reopens this page with the test filled in.

faq.question: How do I open power zones from this FTP?
faq.answer:
Open power zones sends this FTP to the power zones calculator, where you can build Friel, Vance, or Stryd ranges. The card's own table stays the seven Coggan zones: below 55%, 56–75%, 76–90%, 91–105%, 106–120%, 121–150%, and above 150%.

Treat the first number as a starting point. If 250 W × 0.95 gave you 238 W, ride the next intervals from 238 W, then repeat the same protocol before you raise the anchor. A ramp that ends at 320 W becomes 240 W after × 0.75. That is not a reason to rewrite your zones the same day.

faq.question: Which field-test protocol should I use?
faq.answer:
Use the protocol you actually rode. The factor only matches that effort.

For 20 minutes, ride as hard as you can at a pace you can nearly hold and enter the average of those 20 minutes, not a peak. FTP = that average × 0.95. The factor exists because 20 minutes is shorter than the hour FTP stands for, so riders usually hold a higher power. For a ramp, enter the average of the last minute you completed, not a partial minute. FTP = that minute × 0.75. A last minute of 320 W is 240 W FTP. For 2×8, enter the average of both 8-minute efforts, not the better one. FTP = that average × 0.90. An average of 270 W is 243 W FTP. For 60 minutes, enter the hour average. There is no extra multiplier.

The protocol section under the calculator has the basis and the limits for each factor, including the file path, where FTP is critical power × 0.95.

faq.question: Can I use running power in this cycling FTP calculator?
faq.answer: No. Cycling FTP is power at the pedals. Running threshold power, pace, or heart rate comes from another sport. A cycling FTP of 250 W does not set a running zone, and a running pace does not set a cycling watt target. This calculator accepts cycling power data only. For heart rate, running power, or pace threshold, use the lactate threshold calculator.

faq.question: Can I use an indoor test?
faq.answer:
Yes. The same factors apply on a trainer: ×0.95 for 20 minutes, ×0.75 for the last completed ramp minute, ×0.90 for the average of two 8-minute efforts, or the hour average with no factor.

Indoor and outdoor results often differ because of cooling, cadence, and the fact that you cannot coast. Compare a trainer test with another trainer test, and an outdoor test with another outdoor test. A hot room or a trainer that reads high will move the watts as much as the formula. If the trainer says the 20-minute average was 260 W, this page still does 260 × 0.95 = 247 W. It does not correct a bad calibration.

faq.question: What are the limitations?
faq.answer:
The factors correct for duration. They do not fix pacing, a drifting power meter, or one unusual day. Starting the 20 minutes too hard and fading makes the average low. A large anaerobic contribution can leave a 20-minute or ramp estimate high. Ramp tests do that often, because the last minute is a short maximal step: 0.75 × that minute can still sit above the power you can hold for an hour.

One test is a starting point. Repeat the same protocol before you change zones. If you want a model fit across several durations, use the Critical Power calculator. This page's result stays FTP. On the file path, the best window in that one file is what gets used, so a spike harder than the test you meant can raise the estimate.

faq.question: What is FTP (Functional Threshold Power)?
faq.answer:
FTP means Functional Threshold Power: the highest cycling power you can sustain for roughly one hour. It is expressed in watts and, when divided by body weight, as watts per kilogram (W/kg). Cyclists use FTP to set power zones, pace threshold workouts, and compare changes in fitness over time.

This calculator estimates FTP from a 20-minute, ramp, 2×8-minute, or 60-minute field test. It can also estimate FTP from a cycling activity with power data by fitting a power-duration model. Every method is an estimate, so compare repeated tests completed with similar equipment, conditions, and pacing.

faq.question: What is a good FTP?
faq.answer: A useful FTP is one that helps you set appropriate training targets. Absolute watts depend partly on body size, so compare W/kg as well. Use the reference table for context, and compare repeated estimates under similar conditions to follow your own progress.

faq.question: What is a good power-to-weight ratio?
faq.answer: W/kg is FTP divided by body weight in kilograms. For example, 250 W at 70 kg is 3.57 W/kg. It is useful for comparing relative power, especially for climbing; endurance, aerodynamics, and skill also affect performance. The tables above provide context rather than a target everyone must reach.

faq.question: How do FTP power zones work?
faq.answer: Power zones express training intensity as a percentage of FTP. In the Coggan model, endurance is 56–75%, tempo is 76–90%, and threshold is 91–105%. At an FTP of 250 W, tempo is 189–225 W. The result card lists the ranges; the zone calculator offers other models.

faq.question: What is the difference between typing a test and uploading a ride file?
faq.answer: Manual entry converts a known cycling test power using the selected method. File upload extracts two power-duration windows from a cycling activity, fits CP, then uses CP × 0.95 as an FTP approximation. FIT, TCX, and GPX files must contain power data; GPS alone is insufficient.

faq.question: How do I read the result card?
faq.answer: The main number is your estimated FTP in watts. The formula shows how it was calculated. Adding body weight reveals W/kg and a reference band. The manual result card also offers power zones, printing, and a link that preserves your inputs.

faq.question: How do I open power zones from this FTP?
faq.answer: Select “Open power zones” on the result card. Your FTP is carried into the zone calculator, where you can choose another zone model. Use the resulting targets alongside your perceived effort and how consistently you can complete your workouts.

faq.question: Which field-test protocol should I use?
faq.answer: Choose the method matching the test you completed. Do not apply a ramp-test factor to a 20-minute effort. If you have an activity file with suitable power data instead, use the file-estimation option. The test-method section explains the inputs and limitations of each approach.

faq.question: Can I use running power in this cycling FTP calculator?
faq.answer: No. Running and cycling use different movements, devices, and power models. This calculator is designed for cycling power data. Do not use a running-power result to set cycling zones, or transfer cycling FTP directly to running.

faq.question: Can I use an indoor test?
faq.answer: Yes, provided your trainer or power meter records power. Select the method you used outdoors or indoors. Cooling, equipment calibration, and riding position affect results, so keep the setup as consistent as possible when comparing tests.

faq.question: What are the limitations?
faq.answer: These are estimates, not direct physiological measurements. Power-meter accuracy, pacing, fatigue, and the effort recorded all matter. Existing training data can still be useful; a low-effort activity may describe that session better than your maximum capacity. Interpret changes alongside your training history.

details.title: 20-minute test

details.title: 60-minute test

details.title: 3- and 9-minute efforts
details.method: Use the best 3-minute and 9-minute average powers.
details.basis: Two power-duration points are used to fit CP.
details.limits: The activity must cover at least 9 minutes and contain valid power data.

details.title: 30-minute effort

details.basis: CP is fitted from these two windows, not from the last 20 minutes alone.
details.limits: The activity must cover at least 30 minutes. Easy efforts may underestimate your capacity.

details.basis: Running power provides the two points for a running CP estimate.
details.limits: Power and distance are required. This is a running estimate and should not set cycling zones.

faq.question: Can a normal activity file show my max heart rate?
faq.answer:
An observed peak is the highest heart rate in the file that lasted at least one second, after isolated sensor spikes are left out. It is a value you already reached, not a laboratory maximum. One activity is enough, and it does not have to be a race or an all-out test.

A steady ride that holds 176 bpm for two seconds shows an observed peak of 176 bpm. A single sample that jumps more than 20 bpm and disappears is not used.

faq.question: Does the file leave my browser?
faq.answer: The file is parsed in your browser and is not uploaded. Remove the file to clear the observed peak.

faq.question: Why does this disagree with my watch or another formula?
faq.answer:
Each age formula comes from a different sample. At age 40, Tanaka is 180 bpm and Gulati is 171 bpm. A watch may use 220 − age, or a max from another sport.

You choose which ceiling to keep. This page does not change the watch setting.

faq.question: How do I use the result for training?
faq.answer:
The zones on this card use the same %HRmax model as the heart-rate zones calculator. At 180 bpm, Zone 2 is 108–125 bpm.

View heart-rate zones opens that model with your ceiling filled in. Zone 2 alone, and lactate-threshold zones, stay on their own calculators.

faq.question: How far off can an age formula be?
faq.answer:
Tanaka, Monahan, and Seals (2001) reported a standard error of about 10 bpm for 208 − 0.7 × age. Age 40 is 180 bpm, so the Tanaka band on the card is 170–190 bpm.

That band is the study's population error. It is not a personal limit, and it is not applied to Gulati, HUNT, Fox, or Arena. A measured test or an observed peak can sit outside it.

faq.question: Can I save or share this?
faq.answer: Share builds a link with your age, formula, and measured value. Print keeps the scorecard. This page does not write the number into a Trainingload.ai account. Open the app when you want to keep zones there.

faq.question: Does a lower peak mean I am less fit?
faq.answer: No. An easy day, heat, or a sensor that never reached your ceiling produces a lower observed peak. A lower peak does not show a drop in fitness. A peak above the current reference is a reason to look again.

learnHrmax.title: Understand HRmax
learnHrmax.body: HRmax is the highest heart rate you can reach under maximal effort. It’s not a score to chase—think of it as a personal ceiling that helps you structure intensity (e.g., %HRmax zones) and compare your own training over time.

quickAnswer.label: Quick answer
quickAnswer.title: What is maximum heart rate?
quickAnswer.body: Maximum heart rate (HRmax) is the highest heart rate you can reach during a maximal effort. An age formula estimates it; a measured, sport-specific test gives a more individual reference. A common starting point is 208 − (0.7 × age), which estimates 180 bpm at age 40.
quickAnswer.note: Every age-based result is a population estimate, not a personal limit or a fitness score. Compare the formulas, then prefer a reliable measured, sport-specific value when you have one.

measured.value: Use measured HRmax over any formula

byAge.title: Maximum heart rate by age chart
byAge.body: These examples compare three common age-based HRmax equations. Small differences are normal; the spread shows why a calculator should not present one formula as an exact physiological limit.
byAge.caption: Estimated maximum heart rate in beats per minute by age using Tanaka, 220 minus age, and Gulati formulas
byAge.note: Weight and height are not inputs in these validated age-based equations. Resting heart rate is useful for heart-rate reserve and training-zone calculations, but it does not determine HRmax here.

research.title: Research behind the HRmax formulas
research.body: Formula selection and limitations on this page are grounded in peer-reviewed exercise-testing research. The studies report population equations with meaningful individual error, which is why the calculator compares estimates instead of claiming a precise personal maximum.

limitations.title: Limitations of HRmax estimates
limitations.body: Formulas describe population averages and can’t replace your individual test data. Treat the estimate as a starting point: set initial zones, then refine with training and repeatable tests.
items: Large individual variation: genetics, training history, stress, and sleep can change peak results on a given day.
Protocol matters: running vs cycling, step tests, and lab protocols often produce different maxima.
Heart rate isn’t linear: %HRmax zones are a quick setup, but LTHR-based zones are often more actionable for training.
Device and conditions add error: sensor type, fit, temperature, hydration, and altitude can affect readings.

measure.title: How to measure your true HRmax
measure.body: If you want a value closer to your real HRmax, prioritize safety and repeatability over simply going as hard as possible.
steps: Best option: supervised lab test with monitoring (safer and more complete data).
Field test (experienced athletes): warm up well, do progressive intervals, finish with 1–2 near-max efforts, then record the highest sustained heart rate.
Test by sport: HRmax can differ between running and cycling—use sport-specific values if you train both.
Repeat and take the max: perform 2–3 tests on different days and use the highest value as reference.
measure.safety: Stop immediately and seek medical advice if you experience chest pain, dizziness, or unusual discomfort, especially if you have cardiovascular conditions or take related medication.
