fox.name: Fox (1970): 220 − age
fox.summary: The classic, easy-to-remember rule. It’s based on limited historical data and can be inaccurate for many people.

tanaka.name: Tanaka (2001): 208 − 0.7×age
tanaka.summary: A widely used alternative that tends to outperform 220 − age, especially for adults, and is often a good default choice.
tanaka.bestFor: General healthy adults as a default

gulati.name: Gulati (2010): 206 − 0.88×age (women)
gulati.summary: Derived from female samples. Traditional formulas may overestimate HRmax for women; this model is often closer for female athletes.
gulati.bestFor: Women (prefer over general formulas when sex is known)

hunt.name: HUNT / Nes: 211 − 0.64×age
hunt.summary: Based on a large age-spanning cohort, and often considered more reliable for older populations than older rules of thumb.

arena.name: Arena (2015): 209.3 − 0.72×age
arena.summary: Published from a large cohort in exercise testing contexts. Performance is comparable to Tanaka in many settings.

page.medicalDisclaimer: This calculator is for training reference only and is not medical advice. jsonLd.name: VO2max Calculator
jsonLd.description: Free VO2max from Cooper, Rockport, or Beep field tests, plus resting heart rate or a race time. Age- and sex-based fitness norms are included. Not a VDOT race predictor.

faq.name: Is a vo2max calculator the same as a VO2max calculator?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Yes. VO2max and VO2max are common spellings for maximal oxygen uptake, a measure of aerobic capacity. This vo2max calculator estimates it from Cooper, Rockport, Beep, or resting heart rate, with age- and sex-based reference categories. The race option returns VDOT, a running-performance score.

A higher VO2max generally means more oxygen is available to support exercise, but race performance also depends on endurance, running economy, and conditions.

faq.name: Can I use a record that was not an all-out effort?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Yes, if it contains the inputs for the chosen method. A recorded 12-minute running distance can be entered for Cooper; a complete 5K, 10K, or half-marathon time can be used for the race method. You do not need to repeat an activity just to obtain an estimate.

An ordinary training effort may understate your current capacity. Treat the result as a reflection of that record, and keep its effort, route, and conditions alongside it. Comparable records are more useful for tracking change than mixing different methods and conditions.

faq.name: What does 2,800 m on the Cooper test mean?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Cooper VO2max = (distance in meters − 504.9) / 44.73. A 2,800 m 12-minute run is (2800 − 504.9) / 44.73 = 51.3 ml/kg/min. For a 30-year-old man that sits in the very good band, above 48.3 and below 54.0.

Age and sex do not change the Cooper estimate; they select its reference band. Use comparable routes and conditions when repeating it, so distance-measurement error is not mistaken for progress.

faq.name: What does a Rockport walk of 14:30 estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text:
A 30-year-old man at 70 kg who walks 1 mile in 14:30 and finishes at 150 bpm estimates about 44.9 ml/kg/min on the Rockport formula. That is a good band for men aged 30–39, whose good threshold starts at 44.0.

Use a complete one-mile brisk walk, approximately 1.609 km, and the heart rate at its finish. A running time or a recovery heart rate measured several minutes later describes a different effort and changes the meaning of the estimate.

For an adult using the Léger one-minute 20 m protocol, level 10 means 13.0 km/h and about 50.6 ml/kg/min. Equation age is fixed at 18 for adults; younger participants use their actual age.

The protocol starts at 8.5 km/h and adds 0.5 km/h each minute. Shuttle count is recorded only. Scores from other audio versions or 15 m courses cannot be substituted.

faq.name: How does the resting heart rate method work?

acceptedAnswer.text:
VO2max ≈ 15.3 × (max HR / resting HR). Age 30, resting HR 60, and max HR 190 (220 − 30) gives 15.3 × 190 / 60 = 48.5 ml/kg/min. Leave max HR blank to use 220 − age, or enter a measured max.

The coefficient was derived in a specific study population and is not equally accurate for everyone. Sleep, fatigue, caffeine, and posture can affect resting heart rate. An age-predicted maximum heart rate adds another layer of uncertainty.

faq.name: What does a 20:00 5K estimate, and where are training paces?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 20:00 5K gives about 49.8 in the Daniels / Gilbert model. This is a VDOT running-performance score, not a direct gas-analysis measurement of VO2max. It also reflects running economy and endurance. The VDOT calculator provides training paces and equivalent performances.

faq.name: How is a field estimate different from a lab VO2max?

acceptedAnswer.text:
A lab test measures expired gas and is the reference. Cooper, Rockport, Beep, resting heart rate, and race time are estimates. Pacing, heat, sleep, terrain, and the protocol can move the number. Do not treat a field result as a diagnosis or as a watch VO2max.

Watches usually estimate the value from activity data too. Matching units do not make different tests, devices, or models interchangeable. Follow one source over several weeks and compare it with your actual performance.

Cooper, beep, and race efforts are hard. Stop for chest pain, dizziness, or unusual breathlessness. Skip a maximal test if you are not cleared for hard exercise. Use the Rockport walk or resting heart rate when you need a lower-intensity option.

Using an existing record does not require a new hard test. If you choose to retest, select a method appropriate to your current situation. Lower-effort methods still have limitations; this calculator cannot determine whether exercise is safe for you.

faq.name: How often should I retest VO2max?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Retest every 4–8 weeks with the same protocol and similar conditions. A Cooper result is not comparable to a beep result, a resting-HR estimate, or a VDOT score.

There is no need to test every day just to update the number. Keep the route, conditions, and perceived effort with each result. If the change is small, look for it in later comparable records before concluding your fitness has changed.

cooper.explanation: D is distance in metres over 12 minutes. For example, (2800 − 504.9) ÷ 44.73 = 51.3. A 12-minute training effort can also be calculated; an easier effort will usually underestimate maximal capacity.

rockport.explanation: W is weight in pounds, A is age, S is 1 for male or 0 for female, T is time in minutes for one mile, and HR is heart rate at the finish. Kilograms are converted to pounds. Use finish heart rate, not the average for the walk.

beep.explanation: L is the final announced level and v its speed in km/h. A is actual age below 18 and 18 for adults. The original equation studied ages 8–19 and adults 18–50; use outside those populations adds uncertainty. This stage-based estimate does not interpolate shuttle counts. Use only the 8.5 km/h, +0.5 km/h per minute protocol.

restingHr.explanation: HRmax is maximum heart rate and HRrest is resting heart rate. If maximum heart rate is blank, 220 − age is used, adding uncertainty. Measure resting heart rate while awake and at rest; activity average heart rate is not a substitute.

race.explanation: v is speed in metres per minute, t is time in minutes, and f(t) is the sustainable fraction for that duration. The model estimates oxygen demand from speed and adjusts for duration to produce VDOT. Running economy and endurance affect it; it is not a direct VO2max measurement.

definition.title: What is VO2max?
definition.answer: VO2max, or maximal oxygen uptake, is the highest rate at which your body can take in and use oxygen during intense exercise. It describes your aerobic capacity. It is usually expressed in millilitres of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute (ml/kg/min). This calculator estimates it from a field test, heart rate, or running performance.
definition.oxygen: Your lungs bring in oxygen, your heart and blood vessels deliver it, and your working muscles use it to release energy. VO2max reflects the combined capacity of that system. A laboratory exercise test measures oxygen uptake from the air you breathe; a calculator infers it from other measurements.
definition.units: A value of 40 ml/kg/min means 40 millilitres of oxygen per kilogram per minute at maximal effort. For someone weighing 70 kg, that corresponds to 2.8 litres per minute. Relative VO2max accounts for body mass, so a change in weight can change the number even if absolute oxygen uptake stays the same.

endurance.title: Understand aerobic capacity
endurance.text: Running, cycling, and other endurance sports rely on a sustained supply of oxygen. A higher VO2max raises the ceiling for aerobic energy production. How much of that capacity you can sustain also depends on your threshold, movement economy, and endurance.

progress.title: Put progress in context
progress.text: Repeating the same test can help you follow your response to training. Read the estimate alongside pace or power, heart rate, and how the effort felt. One unusually high or low result is less informative than a consistent pattern across comparable tests.

context.title: Keep the score in perspective
context.text: VO2max is one part of cardiorespiratory fitness. It does not describe every aspect of fitness, determine your next race time, or establish whether you are healthy. This field estimate provides training context; clinical assessment needs more information.

interpretation.title: What is a good VO2max for my age?
interpretation.example: For example, 45 ml/kg/min falls in the good band for a man aged 30–39 in this reference table; the very good band starts at 48.3. This is a comparison with age- and sex-based reference values, not an exact percentile or a ranking of people using this calculator.
interpretation.factors: Age, sex, training history, body mass, and the type of exercise all affect interpretation. A reference band is a starting point, not a personal target. To assess your own progress, compare the same method under similar conditions and keep the underlying test record.

education.calculation: Field-test equations relate a measured performance to oxygen uptake observed in a study population. The Cooper test uses 12-minute distance; Rockport combines walk time, finishing heart rate, weight, age, and sex. Heart-rate ratios and race results use different models. Choose the method that matches your record rather than the one that produces the highest score.

accuracy.title: How accurate is a VO2max calculator?
accuracy.intro: A calculator gives an indirect estimate, not a measurement of the oxygen you actually consume. Its usefulness depends on the chosen model, how closely you follow its protocol, and how well the study population represents you. There is no single error percentage that applies to all methods and people.
accuracy.population: For example, the original Rockport study involved healthy adults aged 30–69, while the heart-rate-ratio study involved well-trained men. Using an equation outside its original population adds uncertainty. Estimated maximum heart rate, inaccurate distance, or a different beep-test protocol can introduce further error.
accuracy.vdot: VO2max and VDOT also answer different questions. Laboratory VO2max measures oxygen uptake; VDOT describes running performance and also reflects economy and endurance. The race option here returns that performance-based score. Use a recent race result in the dedicated VDOT calculator when you want training paces and equivalent performances.

improvement.title: How can I improve my VO2max?
improvement.intro: Aerobic fitness responds to regular training, but the size and pace of improvement vary. Build from your current ability and use a routine you can sustain rather than chasing a particular calculator result.

consistency.title: Build a consistent aerobic routine
consistency.text: Choose running, cycling, walking, or another endurance activity that fits your current fitness. Establish manageable, repeatable sessions before adding more work. Consistency gives you a useful baseline for judging whether your training is helping.

intensity.title: Add harder sessions when you are ready
intensity.text: Aerobic interval training can improve VO2max. When you are ready for harder exercise, controlled work periods with recovery can provide a targeted stimulus. The interval research below supports this approach; it does not establish one ideal workout for everyone.

recovery.title: Allow recovery and compare like with like
recovery.text: Balance demanding sessions with easier days and recovery. Use the same test, route, and measurement method when checking progress. Fatigue, heat, and pacing can change a field result without representing a lasting change in aerobic capacity.

improvement.progress: Judge progress over several weeks alongside your actual performance. A faster pace at a similar effort can be useful evidence even when a watch or calculator score barely moves. Keep the test record and training context together before changing your plan.

sources.title: Sources and methodology
sources.intro: These sources cover the physiology, test formulas, and training examples on this page. A published equation can still be less accurate for some people. The Garmin / Cooper Institute source for the age categories is linked beside the table.

notes.fitness: Scientific statement on cardiorespiratory fitness and its assessment.
notes.cooper: Original research relating 12-minute field performance to treadmill oxygen uptake.
notes.rockport: One-mile walking model developed using 343 healthy adults aged 30–69.
notes.heartRate: Heart-rate-ratio model studied in well-trained men; the coefficient is not equally applicable to everyone.
notes.training: A training trial comparing aerobic intervals and continuous training in moderately trained men.
notes.vdot: Explanation of the running-performance score, training paces, and equivalent race performances.
notes.beep: Original one-minute 20 m protocol and age equation, including the adult convention of holding age at 18.
notes.garmin: Manufacturer guidance on running and cycling estimates and the activity data they require.
notes.apple: Manufacturer guidance on cardio fitness estimates and supported outdoor workouts.
notes.trainingDefinitions: Jack Daniels explains the purpose and intensity of easy, threshold, and interval running.

testing.title: How can I estimate VO2max without a lab test?

cooper.setup: A measured, flat course or track, a stopwatch, and a way to record distance. Use this maximal test only if hard running is appropriate for you.
steps: Warm up and identify the start point and distance markers before starting the timer.
Run as far as you can in exactly 12 minutes, pacing the effort so you can sustain it to the end.
Record the distance reached at 12:00, including any partial lap. Cool down after the effort.
cooper.record: Choose Cooper and enter the distance in metres or kilometres. Age and sex select the reference band; they do not change this equation.
cooper.mistake: Entering the distance of a whole activity, stopping the timer during breaks, or treating an easy 12-minute run as a maximal test.

rockport.setup: A flat, accurately measured one-mile course (1.609 km), a stopwatch, your body weight, and a way to measure finishing heart rate.
steps: Warm up, then walk the measured mile as briskly as you can while keeping a walking gait.
Stop the timer at the finish and record heart rate immediately, before it falls during recovery.
Keep the full walking time and finishing heart rate with the test record.
rockport.record: Choose Rockport. Enter age, sex, body weight, one-mile time, and finishing heart rate in bpm. The calculator converts kilograms to pounds for the published equation.
rockport.mistake: Running the mile, substituting average heart rate, or taking a recovery heart rate several minutes after finishing.

beep.setup: Two lines exactly 20 m apart, a flat non-slip surface with room to turn, and audio for the Léger one-minute protocol: 8.5 km/h at level 1, then +0.5 km/h each minute.
steps: Check the audio version and level numbering, measure the course, and warm up.
Run between the lines in time with each beep. Follow that protocol’s stopping rule when you can no longer maintain the pace.
Record the final announced level at which you completed a shuttle, plus the shuttle number if available.
beep.record: Choose Beep and enter that level. The equation uses its speed and age; for adults the equation age is fixed at 18. Shuttle count is retained in the record without partial-stage interpolation.
beep.mistake: Using a 15 m course, a different starting speed, or entering a score such as 10.5 as decimal level 10.5. Record level 10 and shuttle 5 separately.

restingHr.setup: A reliable pulse measurement in bpm and, if already known, a measured maximum heart rate. No new exercise test is required for this method.
steps: Measure while awake after resting quietly, using a consistent posture and time of day.
Repeat on several comparable mornings to check that the value is representative.
Enter resting heart rate and a measured maximum if you have one; otherwise leave maximum heart rate blank for the age-based estimate.
restingHr.record: Choose Resting HR. Use resting bpm, not an activity average. Blank maximum heart rate uses 220 − age, which adds uncertainty.
restingHr.mistake: Using the lowest sleeping pulse, a pulse measured just after exercise, or an unreliable maximum heart rate as though all were equivalent.

race.setup: A recent 5K, 10K, or half-marathon race or maximal time trial with a reliable distance and elapsed time.
steps: Select a record that reflects your current running ability and note the terrain and conditions.
Use the full elapsed finish time, including any stops, rather than moving time or the time of one fast split.
Select the matching event and enter hours, minutes, and seconds.
race.record: The race option returns a Daniels / Gilbert VDOT performance score. Use the dedicated VDOT calculator for training paces and equivalent race performances.
race.mistake: Treating an easy training run as a maximal performance, or interpreting VDOT as a direct measurement of oxygen uptake.

differences.title: Why do my VO2max results differ?
differences.intro: First compare the method and the original record, then consider whether your fitness has changed. Identical units do not make every estimate interchangeable.
differences.sources: For device-specific inputs and supported activities, see the manufacturer explanations.

faq.question: Why is this different from Garmin or Apple Watch?
faq.answer:
A watch estimates VO2max from selected activity and sensor data using its own model. Garmin distinguishes running and cycling estimates; Apple uses eligible outdoor walking, running, and hiking workouts. This calculator instead uses the particular field-test or heart-rate equation you select.

Check the sport, profile information, heart-rate data, and test conditions before comparing values. Follow a consistent source over time rather than averaging unrelated estimates.

faq.question: Why do two calculators disagree on the same test?
faq.answer:
They may use different equations, maximum-heart-rate predictions, units, or test protocols. Beep tests are especially sensitive to the speed schedule and interpretation of level and shuttle scores.

Compare the formula, input definitions, and protocol before comparing the final number. Re-enter the same original record with the same units. A large gap is a reason to check those assumptions, not to choose whichever result is higher.

faq.question: Why am I faster when my VO2max score is unchanged or lower?
faq.answer:
Running performance also depends on economy, sustainable intensity, pacing, and endurance. Your pace can improve without an equally large change in oxygen-uptake capacity. A VDOT score and a watch estimate also respond to different inputs.

Review several comparable sessions and recent test records. Heat, fatigue, terrain, and heart-rate measurement can affect an estimate; one result alone does not establish a lasting change in fitness.

faq.question: Why does another site give me a different fitness category?
faq.answer:
Reference tables can use different populations, age bands, category names, and cutoffs. The same numerical result may therefore receive a different label. This page uses the linked Garmin / Cooper Institute thresholds for its five displayed bands.

Use one reference consistently. The categories are not exact percentiles, and the 20–79 reference range does not independently validate the end-group values for younger or older ages.

training.title: How does VO2max relate to different training sessions?
training.intro: These running examples show what each session is for. Choose the amount of work for your current training base. A VO2max number alone does not specify a safe pace or a complete training plan.

headers.purpose: What it helps with and who it suits

easy.purpose: Build repeatable aerobic volume. Newer runners can use shorter run–walk sessions.
easy.example: 30 minutes of easy running, shortened or broken into run–walk intervals as needed.
easy.intensity: A comfortable conversational effort; adjust for terrain, heat, and recovery.

threshold.purpose: Practise sustaining a controlled demanding effort, for runners already comfortable with regular continuous running.
threshold.example: A 20-minute steady threshold segment, within a session with warm-up and cool-down.
threshold.intensity: Use a recent VDOT threshold pace or a measured threshold reference; avoid turning it into a race.

interval.purpose: Target aerobic power in runners with an established base who are ready for hard sessions.
interval.example: 4 × 4 minutes hard, with 3 minutes of easy active recovery between work bouts.
interval.intensity: Hard but repeatable. Set effort using a suitable training reference; do not sprint to chase a heart-rate target.

training.note: These are separate examples, not a weekly schedule or a requirement to complete all three. Include warm-up and cool-down and allow recovery between demanding sessions. The cited 4 × 4-minute study involved moderately trained men; its protocol is not a universal prescription.

acceptedAnswer.text: VDOT is a performance scale from Jack Daniels’ running formula. It converts a race or time-trial result into a VO2-like score you can use to compare fitness, set training paces, and estimate equivalent race times. It is not a laboratory VO2max measurement.

faq.name: How do I use this VDOT running calculator?

acceptedAnswer.text: Enter a recent race distance and finishing time from a hard, well-paced effort. This VDOT running calculator returns your Daniels VDOT, Easy-to-Repetition training pace ranges, and equivalent predictions from 1500m through the marathon. Compare progress with the same distance when you can.

faq.name: How do I get training paces from VDOT?

acceptedAnswer.text: After you calculate VDOT, the result shows Daniels-style pace ranges for Easy, Marathon, Threshold, Interval, and Repetition running. Use them as reference zones, then adjust for fatigue, heat, hills, and the purpose of the session.

faq.name: Is VDOT the same as VO2max?

acceptedAnswer.text: They are related but not identical. In Daniels’ model, VDOT is a VO2-like performance scale inferred from running results. Use VDOT for race-specific paces; use VO2max when you want aerobic-capacity context.

faq.name: Why do different distances give different VDOT values?

acceptedAnswer.text: Shorter races emphasize speed and anaerobic contribution more, while longer races emphasize endurance and durability. Course and weather also matter. Compare progress using the same distance and similar conditions.

faq.name: How accurate is this VDOT estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a performance-based estimate from your race result and Daniels’ model. Accuracy depends on pacing, course, conditions, and running economy. Use it as a consistent reference and focus on trends.

whatIs.title: What is VDOT?
whatIs.intro: VDOT is a performance scale from Daniels’ running model. It is not the same as a lab-measured VO2max; it converts a race or time-trial result into a VO2-like reference that is useful for comparing performance, estimating training intensity, and tracking long-term trends.

bullets.performance: It comes from performance: the more accurate the distance and the closer the effort is to all-out, the more useful the estimate.
bullets.pacing: It is useful as a pacing anchor: it helps check Easy, Threshold, Interval, and other training intensities.
bullets.trend: It is best used as a trend: compare similar distances and conditions rather than overreacting to one number.

explainer.title: What VDOT is useful for
explainer.intro: VDOT is a performance-based scale that can help you compare results and anchor training paces.

bullets.pacing: Use it to check pacing and compare efforts over time.
bullets.distanceEffect: Different distances can produce different values — that’s normal.
bullets.conditions: Weather, elevation, turns, and pacing strategy can shift the result.

trainingPaces.title: How to use VDOT for training paces
trainingPaces.intro: VDOT is useful because it translates a recent race or test result into training-intensity context. Different paces serve different jobs; they should not all feel like race effort.

easy.title: Easy (E)
easy.text: Used for recovery, aerobic volume, and consistency. It should feel controlled enough that you can train again the next day.

threshold.title: Threshold (T)
threshold.text: Used to improve sustainable intensity. It is close to a hard but controlled effort and should be adjusted when fatigue is high.

interval.title: Interval (I)
interval.text: Used to stimulate VO2max and high aerobic output, often with 3–5 minute repetitions. Quality matters more than forcing every rep.

repetition.title: Repetition (R)
repetition.text: Used for speed, form, and neuromuscular efficiency. Reps are short with generous recovery, not a grinding endurance workout.

trainingPaces.note: The training paces in the result are reference ranges, not strict prescriptions. Adjust for fatigue, weather, terrain, and the purpose of the session.

marathon.title: Marathon (M)
marathon.text: Used for marathon-specific endurance and steady running. It should feel controlled enough to practice fueling and rhythm, not a 5K effort.

vdotVsVo2.title: Is VDOT the same as VO2max?
vdotVsVo2.intro: They are related, but not identical. VDOT is a VO2-like value inferred from running performance, while VO2max is the body’s maximal oxygen uptake capacity.

bullets.vdot: VDOT is affected by running economy, durability, course, weather, and pacing, so it is closely tied to real running performance.
bullets.vo2: VO2max can come from lab gas analysis, field tests such as Cooper/Rockport/Beep, or watch/platform estimates.
bullets.use: Use VDOT when you need running-specific training pace context; use VO2max resources when you want to understand aerobic capacity.

shortAnswer.title: Short answer
shortAnswer.body: VDOT is Jack Daniels’ performance score from a recent race, not a laboratory VO2max. A 5K in 25:00 is VDOT 38.3 here, with E, M, T, I, and R training paces plus equivalent times from 1500 m through the marathon.

method.title: Method & sources
method.description: A recent race goes in. VDOT, Jack Daniels training paces, and a short list of equivalent finish times come out.
method.formula:
VO2 = −4.60 + 0.182258v + 0.000104v², where v is speed in meters per minute.
Fraction of VO2max = 0.8 + 0.1894393e^(−0.012778t) + 0.2989558e^(−0.1932605t), where t is race time in minutes.
VDOT = VO2 / fraction.
Pace ranges use E 59–74%, M 75–84%, T 83–88%, I 95–100%, and R 105–110% of the velocity at that VDOT.
method.examplesNote: A 5K in 25:00 is VDOT 38.3 on this page. A 5K in 20:00 is VDOT 49.8, with a marathon equivalent near 3:11:18. These figures use the equations above. They are not a reprint of the printed VDOT tables, so a small gap versus the V.O2 calculator is expected.
method.assumptions: Use a recent all-out race or time trial on a course whose distance you trust. The model assumes the effort represents your current running fitness and that conditions were ordinary enough to compare later.
method.limits: Heat, altitude, hills, wind, fueling, and pacing change what the same VDOT can produce on race day. Longer equivalents are especially sensitive to durability. Enter a result you ran. A goal time is not a race result.
method.source: Oxygen cost and the fraction of VO2max sustained over time follow the Daniels and Gilbert running equations. The scorecard lists each pace second once where marathon and threshold share the 83–84% shoulder. Compare a result with the official calculator when you need the printed tables:

faqItems.question: What is VDOT?
faqItems.answer: VDOT is a performance scale from Jack Daniels’ running formula. A race or time trial becomes one number you can use to compare fitness, set E, M, T, I, and R training paces, and estimate equivalent finish times. It is not a laboratory VO2max measurement.

faqItems.question: What VDOT is a 20:00 5K?
faqItems.answer: A 20:00 5K is VDOT 49.8 on this calculator, essentially the VDOT 50 band. The same model puts 10K near 41:28, the half marathon near 1:31:50, and the marathon near 3:11:18. Recalculate from a race you actually ran rather than from a goal time.

faqItems.question: What does a VDOT of 38 mean?
faqItems.answer: VDOT 38 is a 5K near 25:10. A 5K in 25:00 is slightly faster, VDOT 38.3. Easy pace is about 6:06–7:16/km, threshold is about 5:18–5:29/km, and the marathon equivalent is about 3:59:30.

faqItems.question: What does a VDOT of 40 mean?
faqItems.answer: VDOT 40 lines up with about 24:06 for 5K, 50:01 for 10K, 1:50:54 for the half marathon, and 3:49:37 for the marathon. Threshold pace is about 5:06–5:16/km (8:12–8:29/mi).

faqItems.question: What marathon time does VDOT 50 predict?
faqItems.answer: VDOT 50 predicts about 3:10:40 for the marathon, 1:31:31 for the half, 41:20 for 10K, and 19:56 for 5K. These are performance equivalents from the Daniels-style equations, not a promise for a hot, hilly, or under-fueled race.

faqItems.question: What is the threshold pace for VDOT 50?
faqItems.answer: For VDOT 50 the modelled threshold range is 4:15–4:24 per km (6:51–7:05 per mile). Interval pace is about 3:50–4:00/km, and repetition is about 3:33–3:41/km. Ranges are percent-of-velocity references, not the single paces in the printed tables.

faqItems.question: Is VDOT the same as VO2max?
faqItems.answer: No. VDOT is inferred from a running result, so economy, pacing, and durability are baked in. VO2max is maximal oxygen uptake from a lab test or a separate field estimate. Use this page for training paces. Use the VO2max calculator when the question is aerobic capacity itself.

faqItems.question: How accurate are the race equivalents?
faqItems.answer: They assume the same VDOT carries to every distance. A 5K in 25:00 returns that 5K, about 51:54 for 10K, 1:19:57 for 15K, 1:55:05 for the half, and 3:57:58 for the marathon at VDOT 38.3. Longer races still depend on durability, fueling, weather, and the course.

faqItems.question: Why do different distances produce different VDOT values?
faqItems.answer: Shorter races lean on speed. Longer races lean on durability, fueling, and pacing. Heat, hills, and a cautious start move the number too. Compare progress on the same distance in similar conditions.

faqItems.question: How often should I recalculate VDOT?
faqItems.answer: Update it after a race or an all-out time trial, not after every easy run. Many runners revisit it every 4–8 weeks of consistent training, and again when fitness has clearly changed. One noisy result should not rewrite every workout.

faqItems.question: Do heat and altitude change the result?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The equations do not add a heat, wind, or altitude correction. A slow race in those conditions produces a lower VDOT than the same fitness would on a cool, flat course. Treat that number as a description of the day, and ease the paces when the next session is also hot or high.

faqItems.question: Can I use a normal training run?
faqItems.answer:
Yes, when the activity contains a 1500 m to marathon effort. Use the whole run, or let the page take the fastest standard race window inside it. You do not need a separate all-out test before a number can be calculated.

A 5 km window in 25:00 is VDOT 38.3. A 20:00 5K is VDOT 49.8.

An easier effort comes out lower. Nothing is added back for fitness you held in reserve.

faqItems.question: Is my activity file uploaded?
faqItems.answer:
The file stays in this browser. FIT, GPX, and TCX are parsed locally, and the page keeps the distance and time it used.

A 10 km file with a 25:00 5K window is scored from that window.

Files over 20 MB, or files without usable timestamps, are skipped.

faqItems.question: Why does this differ from my watch?
faqItems.answer:
A watch often mixes pace, heart rate, and its own model. This calculator uses the race distance and time in the Daniels and Gilbert equations.

A 25:00 5K is VDOT 38.3 here, whatever aerobic number the watch shows for the same run.

Compare the same distance in similar conditions. One hot or hilly day describes that day.

faqItems.question: Can I save or share this VDOT?
faqItems.answer:
Share copies a link to this scorecard. Print keeps the card. Neither writes the number into your training settings.

VDOT 50, about a 19:56 5K, opens again from that link with the same paces.

Using the paces in the app is a separate step you start yourself.

faq: What does a training analysis app need beyond CTL, ATL, and TSB?
It should connect load signals to plan execution, completed workouts, and explicit adjustment drafts so each signal leads to a clear next action.
How should I use PMC when training for a marathon?
Use PMC to monitor load progression and recovery rhythm. If ATL rises too quickly before key sessions, keep frequency but lower intensity to protect consistency.
Why track effective VO2max together with training load?
Load says how much stress you applied. effective VO2max shows how performance response evolves. Together they reduce blind volume and improve adjustment timing.
Can AI marathon training plans replace coach judgment?
AI should draft evidence-based options, not make final calls. The athlete or coach confirms tradeoffs based on goals, fatigue, and race timeline.
answerBlocks: Training load is the stress created by completed workouts over time. It is useful only when it is connected to a plan, recovery, and performance response. A good training load system helps decide whether the next workout should build fitness, hold steady, or allow recovery.
What do CTL, ATL, and TSB mean?

CTL represents longer-term fitness or chronic load, ATL represents short-term fatigue or acute load, and TSB estimates freshness by comparing the two. Together they help athletes understand whether training stress is accumulating sustainably or creating too much near-term pressure.

PMC means Performance Management Chart. In endurance training, a PMC usually plots CTL, ATL, and TSB so athletes can see long-term load, short-term fatigue, and readiness together instead of judging training from one workout or one score.
How do you decide whether to build, hold, or recover?

Do not use one number alone. Build when load is rising gradually and key workouts remain high quality. Hold when fitness is improving but fatigue is close to the edge. Recover when ATL climbs quickly, TSB stays suppressed, or workout quality starts to break down.

metadata.title: PMC Fitness Chart Guide: CTL, ATL, TSB & ACWR Explained
metadata.description: Learn the formulas and practical interpretation of CTL, ATL, TSB, and ACWR on a PMC fitness chart, plus how Trainingload.ai turns load trends into training decisions.

ui.title: PMC Fitness Chart Guide: From CTL, ATL, and TSB to ACWR
ui.subtitle: A Performance Management Chart puts longer-term load, recent load, their difference, and the acute:chronic workload ratio on one timeline. Trainingload.ai then connects the chart to the plan, completed workouts, source activities, and AI review so you can build, hold, recover, or investigate the data.

ui.answerTitle: PMC, CTL, ATL, TSB, and ACWR in 5 short answers
ui.answerSubtitle: Start with the terminology map, then continue to each metric's formula, useful questions, limitations, and combined interpretation.
ui.methodologyTitle: How to use PMC without overfitting the chart
ui.methodologyText: Trainingload.ai treats PMC as load context, not a direct measurement of fitness, fatigue, readiness, or injury risk. CTL, ATL, TSB, and ACWR locate a change; the plan, completed workouts, source activities, threshold and load-source settings, subjective signals, and performance response determine whether a training adjustment is justified.
ui.faqSubtitle: Clear answers to common questions about PMC, CTL, ATL, TSB, and ACWR.

blocks: Read CTL as direction, not urgency
CTL is your long-term load trend. Use it to confirm whether the block is building as intended.
Use ATL as pressure context
ATL shows short-term stress pressure. High ATL is not automatically bad; it must be read with session quality.
Use TSB for timing decisions
TSB helps decide whether to keep, move, or downgrade a key workout before quality drops.
Adjust one variable at a time
When chart signals and execution diverge, change one variable first (intensity, duration, or timing), then review again.
faq: Is a fitness chart the same as PMC?
In endurance training practice, yes. The common fitness-fatigue-form chart is the Performance Management Chart built from CTL, ATL, and TSB.
Should I optimize for higher CTL every week?
No. If CTL rises while key-workout quality and recovery keep deteriorating, the current build may not be working. The goal is sustainable progress, not a nonstop CTL climb.
What if ATL is high but workouts still feel good?
Keep monitoring, but avoid reactive cuts. Confirm with the next key workout and recovery markers before making a large change.
Does a negative TSB mean my form is poor?
Not necessarily. ATL often sits above CTL during a training build, so a negative TSB is common. Consider how long it lasts, key-workout quality, and how you feel before reducing load.
Is there one safe ACWR range for everyone?
No. ACWR only shows whether recent modeled load is high relative to the longer baseline. It cannot predict injury by itself or replace coaching and medical judgment.
Why did my PMC curves jump suddenly?
Check for duplicate activities, threshold changes, a different load source, or an unusually large activity load. Data changes can move CTL, ATL, and ACWR together.
Does a missing workout affect PMC?
Yes. PMC can only use load recorded in the system. Missing workouts understate ATL and CTL; adding them later recalculates the following dates.
How often should I check PMC?
You do not need to watch it constantly. A weekly review, recovery week, race taper, or a clear mismatch between plan and execution are better times to check it.
answerBlocks: What is a PMC fitness chart?

A PMC fitness chart is a Performance Management Chart used to compare long-term fitness, short-term fatigue, and current form. It usually combines CTL, ATL, and TSB so athletes can decide whether to increase load, maintain the plan, or recover before quality drops.
What does CTL show on a PMC chart?

CTL, or chronic training load, shows the longer-term direction of training stress. Rising CTL can indicate building fitness, but it should not be chased blindly. The useful question is whether CTL is increasing while workout quality and recovery remain stable.
What does ATL show on a PMC chart?

ATL, or acute training load, reflects recent training stress and fatigue pressure. High ATL is not automatically bad during a build phase, but it becomes a warning when key workouts suffer, recovery markers decline, or load rises faster than planned.
What does TSB show on a PMC chart?

TSB, or training stress balance, estimates form and freshness by comparing chronic and acute load. A low or negative TSB can be normal in training blocks, but persistent suppression before key sessions may suggest holding load or adding recovery.
What does ACWR show on a PMC chart?

ACWR is the acute:chronic workload ratio. Trainingload.ai calculates it as current ATL divided by current CTL. It can flag a fast change in recent load relative to the longer baseline, but it cannot independently predict injury, recovery, or race readiness.

metrics.name: Chronic Training Load
metrics.summary: CTL is a slow exponentially weighted moving average of daily training load. Trainingload.ai uses a 42-day smoothing period, so CTL is most useful for describing load direction over several weeks: is the current block building, holding, or declining? Interfaces often label CTL as “fitness,” but it measures modeled load history—not how much training the body has absorbed and not a fitness score that can be compared across athletes.
metrics.formula:
decayCTL = exp(-1 / 42)
CTLtoday = CTLyesterday × decayCTL
           + daily load × (1 − decayCTL)
metrics.interpretation: Read CTL direction and slope against the training block. A gradual rise with stable key-session execution suggests load is accumulating as intended. A sudden jump should trigger a check for an unusual activity, threshold edit, duplicate record, or load-source change. There is no universal ideal CTL value.
metrics.caution: Rising CTL does not prove successful adaptation, and higher is not automatically better. The same CTL can come from different sports, intensity distributions, and data sources.

metrics.name: Acute Training Load
metrics.summary: ATL is the fast exponentially weighted moving average of the same daily load series. Trainingload.ai uses a 7-day smoothing period, making it sensitive to recent sessions and useful for locating when short-term training pressure rose or fell. Interfaces often call ATL “fatigue,” but ATL does not read sleep, pain, illness, or subjective fatigue. It provides fatigue context rather than a physiological diagnosis.
metrics.formula:
decayATL = exp(-1 / 7)
ATLtoday = ATLyesterday × decayATL
           + daily load × (1 − decayATL)
metrics.interpretation: When ATL rises quickly, inspect the last 7–14 days of long sessions, quality workouts, races, and unplanned activity. Decide whether the increase matches the plan. ATL normally falls faster than CTL during a recovery week. The important question is whether the ATL change also coincides with worse execution, subjective state, or pain signals.
metrics.caution: High ATL is not automatically dangerous, and low ATL does not prove good recovery. It describes recent load, not measured fatigue.

metrics.name: Training Stress Balance
metrics.summary: TSB is the difference between current CTL and ATL. It describes where recent load sits relative to the slower load trend. A negative value means ATL is above CTL, which is common during a build; a positive value means ATL is below CTL, which is common during recovery or tapering. TSB is often labeled “form” or “freshness,” but it remains a mathematical relationship between 2 load models.
metrics.interpretation: Use TSB as timing context. During a taper, ATL falls faster and TSB rises; during a build, ATL rises faster and TSB becomes negative. Before a key workout or race, compare the pattern with the athlete's own history, plan purpose, execution quality, and subjective state rather than applying universal positive or negative bands.
metrics.caution: Positive TSB does not prove peak readiness, and negative TSB does not diagnose overtraining. A fixed “optimal range” is not portable across athletes and load models.

metrics.name: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio
metrics.summary: ACWR, also written as A:C Ratio, compares recent load with the longer load baseline. Trainingload.ai divides current ATL by current CTL, which is not the same as every 7-day-total / 28-day-average implementation found online. A higher ratio only confirms that modeled recent load is higher relative to the longer baseline; it is useful for locating a ramp or a possible data anomaly.
metrics.formula:
ACWRtoday = ATLtoday / CTLtoday
if CTLtoday = 0, return 0
metrics.interpretation: Read the ATL and CTL absolute values before the ratio. ACWR can rise because of a planned overload, one abnormal activity, a small denominator after a long break, a threshold edit, or a duplicate import. After verifying the data, combine sport impact, pain, illness, sleep, and workout quality before changing training.
metrics.caution: ACWR is not an injury predictor, and no universal “safe sweet spot” applies to every athlete. Display bands are review prompts, not medical or training clearance.

patterns: Planned load build
CTL rises gradually; ATL is periodically above CTL; TSB is moderately negative; ACWR stays near the athlete's recent pattern.
Load is accumulating without an obvious acceleration signal.
If key-session quality, subjective state, and recovery remain stable, keep the plan. Do not add load merely to make the chart look better.
Recent load acceleration
ATL rises quickly; CTL lags; TSB drops; ACWR rises at the same time.
Recent modeled load is clearly above the longer baseline, but the cause and athlete response still need verification.
Trace the source workouts and rule out duplicates or threshold changes. If key-session quality also declines, change only one variable: intensity, duration, or timing.
Recovery week or taper
ATL falls faster than CTL; TSB rises; ACWR falls; CTL usually holds or declines slowly.
Recent load is decreasing and modeled freshness is rising, but peak condition is not proven.
Validate with a comparable key session, subjective feedback, and event demands. Do not panic-add load because CTL dipped slightly.
Break, missed training, or missing data
ATL and CTL both fall; TSB may become positive; ACWR is low or distorted by a small CTL denominator.
The model sees less training load but cannot distinguish planned rest, missing records, injury, or a schedule interruption.
Check activity completeness and load sources first. Do not treat positive TSB as proof of good form.
Chart and athlete disagree
PMC appears normal while pace/power execution, sleep, pain, or subjective fatigue keeps worsening.
The load model is missing important context; the chart alone cannot justify more pressure.
Treat the conflict as an investigation signal and keep changes conservative. Prioritize health and qualified advice for pain, illness, or abnormal symptoms.
advantages: Core PMC charts and trends are free
The Free plan includes PMC, CTL–ATL–TSB charts, the metrics hub, and the deeper dashboard workspace. Evaluate the workflow with your own history before paying for core load analysis.
Transparent formulas, thresholds, and load sources
Trainingload.ai documents its 7-day ATL, 42-day CTL, TSB, and ACWR formulas. Activity load can use power, heart rate, pace, or session RPE according to your thresholds and source priority.
Trace the curve back to plan and completed work
The chart is not an isolated smooth line. Connect a PMC change to planned sessions, completed work, missed workouts, and source activities before explaining what changed.

PMC describes applied pressure. Effective VO2max, threshold trends, workout quality, and subjective signals help test whether the expected response occurred—reducing the temptation to chase CTL alone.
AI drafts changes; you approve the result
When load and execution evidence support an adjustment, the AI coach can draft a conservative change inside the current plan. Review the reason, exact edit, and validation point before applying it.

sources: Performance Management Chart: CTL, ATL, and TSB model concepts.
Endurance coaching practice: validate chart signals with workout execution and recovery.
Trainingload.ai product method: make one conservative adjustment, then review the next key session.

ui.title: Power Curve analysis for CP, FTP, and training load decisions
ui.subtitle: Use your Power Curve to see where performance is improving, where it plateaus, and how that should change your next block.
ui.blocksTitle: How to use Power Curve in weekly decisions
ui.blocksSubtitle: Read changes by duration, then connect them to CP/FTP and zone targets before adjusting workouts.
ui.ctaTitle: Turn power-duration data into clear training actions.
ui.ctaText: Compare curve shape over time, check CP and FTP context, and adjust intensity distribution with less guesswork.

blocks: Check short vs long duration changes
Separate sprint, VO2, and threshold windows so you can identify which system is improving or lagging.
Validate CP/FTP from curve behavior
If threshold-duration segments flatten, recheck CP/FTP assumptions before forcing higher zone targets.
Adjust only one variable first
When curve and workout quality disagree, adjust intensity or duration first, then review the next key session.
Use curve trends, not one-day spikes
A single peak effort can be noisy. Direction across weeks is more useful for planning decisions.
faq: Is Power Curve the same as Power Duration Curve?
In practice yes. Most athletes use Power Curve as a shorthand for a power-duration best-effort curve.
Should I update zones after every new peak?
No. Use trend consistency and execution quality before changing zones aggressively.
Can runners use Power Curve too?
Yes. Running power users can apply the same duration-based analysis logic as cyclists.

metadata.description: Use Power Rankings to benchmark your best efforts by duration and monitor performance trends across training blocks.

ui.title: Power Rankings by duration for cleaner performance benchmarking
ui.subtitle: Track where your strongest durations are, where you lag, and how rankings shift as training load changes.
ui.blocksSubtitle: Benchmark by duration, compare blocks, and prioritize one targeted limiter at a time.
ui.ctaTitle: Benchmark performance without losing training context.
ui.ctaText: Use rankings as a directional signal, then validate changes with plan execution and load response.

blocks: Rank by meaningful durations
Use fixed windows like 1 min, 5 min, 20 min, and 60 min to compare changes in energy systems.
Compare blocks, not random weeks
Block-to-block comparison reduces noise and better reflects whether the current plan is working.
Link ranking drift to training load
If rankings drop while load rises, review recovery and intensity distribution before adding volume.
Choose one limiter each cycle
Do not chase every weak duration at once. Select one limiter and build the block around it.
faq: Are Power Rankings only for cyclists?
No. Any sport with reliable power-duration data can use this framework.
Should rankings replace CP and FTP?
No. Rankings complement CP/FTP and help interpret where specific duration strength is changing.
How often should I review rankings?
Weekly scanning is fine, but major training decisions should rely on block-level trends.

ui.ctaTitle: Keep zone targets aligned with real execution.
ui.ctaText: Calibrate zones using threshold evidence and block goals so daily workouts stay specific and sustainable.

blocks: Use test evidence first
Anchor custom boundaries to recent tests, not historical assumptions from a different fitness phase.
Align zones with block objective
Base periods, build phases, and race prep often require different emphasis even with similar thresholds.
Keep naming and labels consistent
Consistent labels make workout prescriptions and post-session reviews easier to interpret.
Recheck after major adaptation
When threshold and execution quality shift materially, recalibrate zones to avoid stale targets.
faq: Should I always use model-based zones?
No. Model zones are a good start, but custom zones can fit better when you have reliable test data.
How often should I update custom zones?
Usually per block or after a meaningful threshold change, not after every isolated workout.
Can I mix custom zones across sports?
Yes. Running and cycling can use different zone boundaries when their threshold behavior differs.

ui.blocksSubtitle: Treat CP, FTP, and LTHR as starting points, then validate them against workout execution and fatigue response.
ui.ctaTitle: Use threshold estimates as decision inputs, not single-point truth.
ui.ctaText: Combine CP, FTP, and LTHR evidence with execution quality to set more stable zone targets.

blocks: Start with recent representative data
Use recent workouts or tests from the current training phase to avoid stale threshold references.
Compare multiple estimate paths
File-based and model-based estimates should be directionally aligned before making a big zone update.
Apply small calibration steps
Adjust thresholds conservatively first, then validate with key-session quality and perceived effort.
Re-estimate on block transitions
Thresholds can drift across blocks. Recheck before entering build or race-specific phases.
faq: Should CP and FTP always match closely?
Not exactly. They often track similarly, but method and data quality can create a meaningful gap.
Can LTHR be estimated without lab testing?
Yes. Field-test and workout-derived methods can provide practical estimates for training decisions.
Do I need to update thresholds every week?
Usually no. Update when trend evidence supports change, not on isolated good or bad sessions.

metadata.title: effective VO2max Trend Analysis for Training Decisions
metadata.description: Track effective VO2max trend with training load context and turn fitness response signals into safer plan adjustments.

ui.title: effective VO2max trend analysis for training decisions
ui.subtitle: Read effective VO2max as a response signal, not a vanity score, by combining it with CTL, ATL, TSB, and workout execution.
ui.blocksTitle: How to read effective VO2max trend
ui.blocksSubtitle: Use trend direction, load pressure, and session quality together before changing plan intensity.
ui.ctaTitle: Use VO2 trend to validate adaptation, not chase noise.
ui.ctaText: When trend and load diverge, make one conservative change and verify with the next key workout.

blocks: Use weekly direction over daily noise
Single-day jumps can be noisy. Weekly and block-level direction is more reliable for planning.
Pair trend with CTL and ATL
If trend stalls while ATL remains elevated, reduce stress before adding more volume.
Check execution quality before edits
Trend drops are more actionable when they align with degraded key-session quality.
Apply one adjustment at a time
Keep frequency stable, change one variable, and reassess after the next quality session.
faq: Is effective VO2max enough to change my plan?
No. It should be combined with load and execution signals before modifying training targets.
How often should I review effective VO2max trend?
A quick daily scan is fine, but weekly and block reviews drive better decisions.
Can trend decline happen even with high training load?
Yes. Excess stress or poor recovery can suppress adaptation despite high load volume.

metadata.title: Best Efforts Analysis for Pace, Power, and Progression Checks
metadata.description: Review Best Efforts across durations and connect peak performances to training blocks, load, and pacing decisions.

ui.title: Best Efforts analysis for pace, power, and progression checks

ui.blocksTitle: How to use Best Efforts properly
ui.blocksSubtitle: Group by duration, compare by block, and connect results with execution context before changing targets.
ui.ctaTitle: Best efforts are signals, not complete decisions.
ui.ctaText: Blend best-effort changes with load and recovery context to set smarter weekly priorities.

blocks: Analyze by duration families
Short, medium, and long durations reflect different systems and should not be mixed into one verdict.
Compare block baselines
Block-level baselines reduce noise and reveal whether current training is moving the right limiter.
Cross-check with load context
If best efforts improve but fatigue accumulates too quickly, maintain gains before adding more stress.
Use for priority setting
Select one weak duration family as the next block priority instead of chasing every metric.
faq: Are best efforts enough for threshold updates?
Not alone. Use them with CP/FTP/LTHR trend evidence before making substantial threshold changes.
Why did my best effort improve but race pace did not?
Peak efforts and race durability can diverge; pacing, fatigue resistance, and specificity still matter.
How often should I review best efforts?
Weekly scans are useful, but block-level interpretation is more reliable for plan edits.

metadata.title: Fitness, Fatigue, and Form for Weekly Load Decisions
metadata.description: Use Fitness, Fatigue, and Form (CTL/ATL/TSB) to manage training load and make practical weekly adjustments.

ui.title: Fitness, Fatigue, and Form for weekly load decisions
ui.subtitle: Translate CTL, ATL, and TSB into practical actions for recovery timing, quality-session scheduling, and risk control.
ui.blocksSubtitle: Read trend direction, short-term pressure, and freshness together before adjusting workload.
ui.ctaTitle: Use form signals to choose timing, not panic.
ui.ctaText: When fatigue rises and form drops, make one conservative change and protect the next key session quality.

blocks: Fitness (CTL) for long-term direction
Use CTL to check whether your block is progressing, not to force continuous increases.
Fatigue (ATL) for short-term pressure
Use ATL to judge near-term stress and decide whether workload needs temporary relief.
Form (TSB) for session timing
Use TSB to decide whether to keep, move, or reduce key sessions before quality breaks down.
Change one variable, then recheck
Frequency, intensity, or duration: adjust one first, then validate against the next key workout.
faq: Is Fitness/Fatigue/Form the same as PMC?
Yes, in most endurance contexts this naming maps directly to CTL/ATL/TSB-based PMC logic.
Does low form always mean no hard workouts?
Not always. Context matters. Evaluate recovery state, session priority, and recent execution quality.
How should beginners use this chart?
Keep it simple: avoid sudden spikes, preserve consistency, and make conservative adjustments.

faq: How many weeks should a 10K training plan be?
This schedule is 10 weeks. Eight weeks can work if you already run longer than 50 minutes easy; 12 weeks means adding base weeks before week 1, not compressing the long-run build.
Is this a beginner 10K training plan?
Yes, for a first-time finisher who can already complete an easy 5K or about 30–40 minutes continuously. If that base is missing, use Couch to 5K or the finish 5K plan first.
How many runs per week are in this program?
Three. Two easy runs and one long run, with a short steady block only in weeks 4, 6 and 8, and rest between them.
What is the longest run in this 10-week schedule?
65 minutes in week 7, kept conversational. Walk breaks are allowed; it is time on feet, not a dress-rehearsal race.
Do I need threshold or interval training?
No. This completion plan uses controlled RPE 5–6 steady running only in weeks 4, 6 and 8. It is not a threshold or interval workout.
Can I walk during the final 10K?
Yes. Start conservatively and take short walk breaks whenever needed; completing the distance matters more than forcing a pace.

faq: Is this Couch to 5K plan really free?
Yes. The complete nine-week schedule is free to read and follow here. You can also add the official plan to your calendar for free, record workouts, and make manual changes.
Do I need an account to follow the plan?
No. You only need an account if you want to save the plan to your calendar and track it in Trainingload.ai.
How long does Couch to 5K take?
This plan takes nine weeks, with three run-walk sessions per week. Repeat a week when the running segments are not yet controlled.
How many days a week will I run?
Three. Keep the days non-consecutive when possible so that each run-walk session has recovery around it.
Can I repeat a week if it feels too hard?
Yes. Repeat the week or add recovery instead of forcing the next progression. Pain, illness, or an altered gait calls for stopping and getting appropriate advice.
Is C25K the same as Couch to 5K?
C25K is a common abbreviation for Couch to 5K. Different programs may use different wording or timing, so follow one complete progression consistently rather than mixing weeks from several plans.
What should I do if I miss a workout?
Usually skip it or move it while preserving recovery. Do not squeeze two run-walk sessions into one day or cram every missed workout into the weekend.
Can I do this Couch to 5K plan on a treadmill?

Yes. Keep the same run-walk times and use a comfortable speed rather than copying an outdoor pace. A small incline is optional, not required. Hold the rails only for stepping on or off, and stop if your gait changes.
Is there a free Couch to 5K app?

You can follow the complete plan on this page without an app. Sign in to Trainingload.ai to add the same plan to the Web and iOS calendars for free, see today's workout, and record completion. AI coaching is optional.
Can AI Coach adjust the plan for me?

AI Coach can use completed training, load and recovery to generate an adjustment suggestion. You review the reason and confirm it before the calendar changes, and you can always adjust the plan manually.
Is this a Couch to 5K AI plan?

The schedule itself is a complete free 9-week Couch to 5K plan. AI coaching is optional: it can suggest repeating a week or moving a session when completed runs and recovery say the next step is too hard. Nothing changes until you confirm.

collection.faqSubtitle: Quick answers for athletes comparing an AI running coach, AI cycling coach, and adaptive endurance training tools.
faq: What is an AI endurance coach?
An AI endurance coach reviews training plans, completed workouts, training load, and performance response to help runners and cyclists decide what to do next.
Is this different from a chatbot?
Yes. A useful AI coach needs training context: the plan, the workout history, the load trend, and the next sessions that might need adjustment.
Should one AI coach cover both running and cycling?
It can, but the interpretation should differ by sport. Running creates more impact stress, while cycling often depends more on power, FTP, and ride-specific fatigue.
Can AI replace a human coach?
No. AI can summarize evidence and draft options, but goals, health, race priorities, and final training decisions still need human judgment.

running-coach.definitionTitle: What is an AI running coach?
running-coach.definitionText: An AI running coach is software that reviews a runner's plan, completed runs, training load, pace, heart rate, and recent performance response to suggest the next training decision. The useful version is not just a chatbot: it connects real workout data to plan adjustments that the runner or coach can confirm.
running-coach.promise: Good running advice connects mileage, intensity, impact stress, and recovery before changing the next workout.
running-coach.exampleSubtitle: A concrete review pattern helps the page answer how AI coaching works, not just what the feature is called.
exampleSteps: The runner missed Sunday's long run, completed two easy runs, and still has a threshold workout planned for tomorrow.
ATL is rising faster than planned, TSB is still negative, heart-rate drift was high on the last easy run, and effective VO2max has not improved this week.
Keep the run frequency, replace the threshold workout with 35-45 minutes easy, and move the key session later only if the next easy run is stable.
The change remains a draft until the athlete or coach confirms it against race timeline, soreness, sleep, and injury risk.

running-coach.dataSubtitle: The strongest running-coach page should show exactly which inputs turn into a decision.

Shows the intended stimulus and where the session sits in the week.
Decide whether to keep, move, reduce, or replace the workout.

Compare planned and actual execution before interpreting load.
ATL / CTL / TSB
Separates short-term fatigue, longer-term load, and freshness.
Avoid adding intensity when fatigue is already ahead of the plan.
Pace and grade-adjusted pace
Terrain and hills can make the same pace mean different stress.
Judge whether the run was truly easy, steady, threshold, or too hard.
Heart-rate drift
A rising heart rate at stable pace can signal heat, fatigue, or weak aerobic durability.
Reduce intensity or extend recovery before the next key session.

Decide whether to build, hold, or recover in the next microcycle.
running-coach.signalsTitle: Running signals the AI coach should read
running-coach.signalsSubtitle: Running is not only about weekly distance. The coach should interpret load, pace, terrain, and recovery together.
signals: Missed long runs, shortened intervals, and swapped easy days change what the next week can safely absorb.
ATL, CTL, and TSB help identify whether fatigue is rising faster than fitness or whether the plan can keep building.
Flat pace, grade-adjusted pace, and aerobic decoupling can show whether an easy run stayed easy or became costly.
Performance trend gives context for whether the block is working, stagnating, or being hidden by fatigue.

faq: Can an AI running coach build a marathon plan?
Yes, but the useful part is not only generating the plan. It should also review completed long runs, load buildup, and recovery before drafting adjustments.
What makes running different from cycling for AI coaching?
Running load includes impact stress. A similar TSS score can feel more damaging in running than cycling, so recovery and frequency need sport-specific interpretation.
Should AI change a missed running workout automatically?
No. The safer workflow is to explain the tradeoff, draft the change, and let the athlete or coach confirm it.
Which running metrics matter most?
Plan completion, long-run progression, easy-run control, threshold work, ATL/CTL/TSB, pace zones, heart-rate drift, and effective VO2max are all useful together.

faq: Can an AI cycling coach use FTP?
Yes. FTP and CP help anchor power zones, workout targets, and training-load interpretation, especially when reviewing threshold and VO2max work.
What cycling data should AI review?
Useful inputs include planned ride targets, completed duration, average power, Normalized Power, variability, heart rate, FTP or CP, and load trends.
How should AI handle an unplanned hard group ride?
It should treat the ride as real training stress, explain the tradeoff, and draft a recovery or intensity adjustment for the next session.
Is cycling training load easier to compare than running load?
Power makes cycling load more measurable, but fatigue still depends on context, fueling, terrain, heat, and the rider's recent training history.

faq.question: Is my workout stored?
faq.answer: No. The MVP processes the file in memory and does not persist the file, evidence bundle, route, or AI result.

faq.question: Which workout files can I upload?
faq.answer: You can upload one FIT, GPX, or TCX activity up to 25 MB. FIT usually contains the richest sensor data; GPX and TCX depend on what the exporting device or platform includes.

faq.question: What if my file has no GPS, heart rate, or power?
faq.answer: The review continues with the data that is actually present. Without GPS there is no 3D route; without heart rate or power, the review clearly states that those conclusions are unavailable.

faq.question: How are running pace and speed displayed?
faq.answer: Running speed is converted to minutes per kilometre, such as 5:30/km. Cycling and other speed-based activities use kilometres per hour. Raw metres per second are not shown in the review.

faq.question: How accurate is the AI workout review?
faq.answer: It is only as complete as the uploaded activity and the optional threshold values you provide. The review cites available aggregates and derived trends, but one workout cannot establish long-term fitness or recovery.

faq.question: Why might this differ from my watch or training platform?
faq.answer: Devices and platforms may use different smoothing, pause handling, zones, and proprietary algorithms. This tool explains the uploaded data; it does not replace the source platform's calculations.

faq.question: Why is the route not on a map?
faq.answer: The 3D view deliberately has no basemap. It preserves route shape, elevation, and speed while removing the geographic origin.

faq.question: Is the review always free?
faq.answer: The current version offers each visitor up to 3 complete reviews per rolling 24 hours without an account or API key, subject to fair use and the platform’s rolling shared capacity. Each used review recovers 24 hours after use.

faq.question: How are my free reviews counted and restored?
faq.answer: Each visitor can complete up to 3 free reviews in any rolling 24-hour period; there is no calendar-day or midnight reset. Each successful review is restored separately 24 hours after it finishes. A failed generation does not use one of your successful-review allowances.

faq.question: What is the shared free capacity?
faq.answer: All anonymous visitors share a rolling free-capacity pool to keep this tool sustainable. Capacity used by each successful review returns 24 hours later, so you may need to wait even when personal reviews remain. This allowance is separate from member AI credits.

faq.question: What does the full Trainingload.ai app add?
faq.answer: The free tool reviews one isolated workout. The full app keeps your activities together so you can analyse training load, fitness trends, recovery, plans, and repeated AI reviews over time.

faq.question: Is this medical advice?
faq.answer: No. It is training-data interpretation, not medical diagnosis or individualized medical advice.

faq.question: How do I open a FIT file?
faq.answer: Choose a .fit file or drag it into this FIT file viewer. The file opens locally in your browser—nothing is uploaded. You can then inspect the activity summary, 3D route, Record charts, CRC checks, and FIT messages.

faq.question: What is a FIT file?
faq.answer: FIT stands for Flexible and Interoperable Data Transfer. It is a compact binary format used by Garmin and many fitness devices for activities, workouts, courses, health data, settings, and other sports data.

faq.question: Is my FIT file uploaded?
faq.answer: No. The file is read entirely on your device. It is not uploaded, and Trainingload.ai never receives the file bytes or decoded contents.

faq.question: Is a FIT file reader the same as a FIT file viewer?
faq.answer: Yes. Both names describe this local tool: it opens a FIT file in your browser so you can read messages and summaries. It does not convert or upload the file.

faq.question: Which FIT files can this viewer open?
faq.answer: It can inspect standard FIT files recognized by the official Garmin FIT JavaScript SDK, including activity, workout, course, wellness, and device-related files up to 25 MB.

faq.question: What does a failed CRC check mean?
faq.answer: It means the file signature, declared size, header CRC, or file CRC did not pass Garmin SDK integrity checks. The file may be incomplete, corrupted, or exported in a non-standard way; partial messages may still be readable.

faq.question: Can I view FIT developer fields?
faq.answer: Yes. The decoder includes recognized developer-defined fields and reports how many developer field descriptions were encountered.

faq.question: How do I calculate running pace?
faq.answer: Divide time by distance in matching units. For example, 25 minutes over 5 kilometers is 5:00 min/km. To find time, multiply pace by distance; to find distance, divide time by pace.

faq.question: How do I convert min/km to min/mile?
faq.answer: Multiply the pace in seconds per kilometer by 1.609344, then convert the result back to minutes and seconds. For example, 5:00 min/km is about 8:03 min/mile. Divide by 1.609344 to go the other way.

faq.question: What pace do I need for a 4-hour marathon?
faq.answer: Divide 4 hours by 42.195 km. The average is about 5:41 min/km or 9:09 min/mile, rounded to the nearest second. To finish under four hours, aim slightly faster than the exact average and account for stops.

faq.question: Can I convert treadmill speed to running pace?
faq.answer: Yes. Divide 60 by speed in km/h to get minutes per kilometer: 12 km/h is 5:00 min/km. Divide 60 by mph for minutes per mile. This is a unit conversion; it does not adjust for treadmill calibration, incline or outdoor conditions.

faq.question: Is 5:30 the same as 5.30 minutes?
faq.answer: No. 5:30 means 5 minutes and 30 seconds, which is 5.5 minutes. A decimal value of 5.30 minutes is 5 minutes and 18 seconds. Enter minutes and seconds in their separate fields.

faq.question: What is a good running pace for a beginner?
faq.answer: There is no single pace that suits every beginner. Distance, experience, terrain and the purpose of the run all matter. For an easy run, focus on a comfortable effort you can sustain rather than chasing a pace from a comparison table.

faq.question: Why is my watch showing a different pace?
faq.answer: Check whether you are comparing instant pace or average pace, and moving time or elapsed time. GPS distance and rounding can also differ. For a race goal, elapsed time and the official course distance provide a consistent starting point.

faq.question: Does the chart predict my marathon time from a 5K?
faq.answer: The chart applies the same pace to each distance. Predicting a marathon from a 5K result needs a performance model and assumptions about endurance preparation. Follow the race time predictor link for that estimate.

faq.question: Where can I calculate easy, tempo and interval paces?
faq.answer: Use the VDOT calculator with a recent race result for training pace guidance. The pace needed for a desired finish time is not automatically the right pace for every training run.

faq.question: Can I print or share my result?
faq.answer: Yes. Print the result card or share a link that restores your inputs. The 5 km example is labeled as sample data. Calculating or sharing a result does not automatically save it to your Trainingload account.

definition.title: What is running pace?
definition.answer: Running pace is the time you take to cover one kilometer or one mile. A pace of 5:00 min/km means five minutes per kilometer. A smaller pace number means you are running faster.
definition.detail: Pace describes a completed run or the average you need for a goal time. It does not tell you how hard that pace will feel, or whether you can hold it over a longer distance.

formulas.title: How to calculate running pace, time and distance
formulas.intro: Enter the two values you know to find the third. Keep distance and pace in matching units: kilometers with min/km, or miles with min/mile.
formulas.clockNote: Read 5:30 as five minutes and thirty seconds, or 5.5 minutes. It is not 5.30 minutes. The calculator has separate minute and second fields to keep this clear.

conversion.title: Running pace conversion: min/km, min/mile, km/h and mph
conversion.body: Pace measures time per distance; speed measures distance per time. As speed goes up, the pace number goes down. Use this chart to compare watch settings or convert a treadmill speed into running pace.
conversion.caption: Running pace and speed conversion chart
conversion.formula: To convert min/km to min/mile, multiply by 1.609344. For speed in km/h, divide 60 by your pace in minutes per km. To go back, divide 60 by km/h. The same relationship connects min/mile and mph.
conversion.note: One mile is exactly 1.609344 km. Paces are rounded to the nearest second and speeds to two decimal places.

goals.title: Race pace charts for common finish times
goals.body: Find the average pace for a target finish time, then use that time and distance in the calculator to build kilometer or mile splits. These are goal-time conversions, not predictions from your current fitness.
goals.caption: {race}: finish time and average pace
goals.note: Goal paces are rounded to the nearest second for display; calculations use the full value. If you want to finish under a target, aim slightly faster than its exact average and allow for any stops.
goals.tableHint: On a narrow screen, swipe the table sideways if needed.

reading.title: How to read your pace and split times

items.title: Average pace and instant pace
items.body: Average pace is total time divided by total distance. Your watch’s instant pace describes a shorter window and can fluctuate with GPS reception, turns and changes in speed. Compare like-for-like averages when reviewing a run.

items.title: Moving time or elapsed time?
items.body: Use moving time to describe the pace while you were moving. For a race goal, use elapsed time, including stops. Aid stations and other pauses still count toward your finish time.

items.title: The final partial kilometer or mile
items.body: A marathon is 42.195 km and a half marathon is 21.0975 km. The last split can therefore be shorter than a kilometer or mile. The split column shows that section’s time; elapsed time shows the cumulative time from the start.

items.title: Combining runs or unequal splits
items.body: Add all times and all distances, then divide total time by total distance. For example, 6 km at 5:00/km plus 4 km at 6:00/km gives an average of {weightedPace}/km. Taking the simple average of 5:00 and 6:00 would give the wrong result.

items.title: Even, positive and negative splits
items.body: Even splits keep the same pace. A positive split means the second half takes longer than the first; a negative split means it takes less time. This calculator builds even splits. Hills, weather, stops and pacing choices can change the actual pattern.

next.title: Choosing a pace you can sustain
next.body: A goal time tells you the pace required, but choosing a realistic goal also needs recent performance and preparation. Use these tools when you want training paces or an estimate based on another race.
