faq.question: Can I send this workout to a Garmin watch?
faq.answer:
A workout FIT file is a structured session the watch can follow. It is separate from a completed activity file.

Example: 10 minutes easy, 5 repeats of 3 minutes hard and 2 minutes easy, then 10 minutes easy is 45:00.

The file has no GPS track. Send the .fit file with Garmin Connect.

faq.question: How do I use this in intervals.icu?
faq.answer:
intervals.icu reads the workout FIT file and the workout_doc JSON from Copy intervals.icu JSON.

Example: the 45:00 run is duration 2700, with a 600-second warm-up, 5 repeats, and a 600-second cool-down.

Upload the FIT file or paste the JSON into a calendar workout. Cycling Z4 is written as 95% FTP.

faq.question: How do pool distances work?
faq.answer:
Set the sport to swimming and the step unit to meters.

Example: 200 m warm-up, 8 repeats of 100 m hard and 20 seconds rest, then 200 m cool-down.

The FIT file stores those as distance steps. The on-screen clock uses a 6:00/km preview only so the timeline has a width.

faq.question: Does my workout file get uploaded?
faq.answer:
Importing a FIT or JSON workout stays in this browser.

Example: choose Import FIT or JSON and pick a workout file. The steps open in the builder.

The file is not uploaded. Files over 20 MB are refused.

faq.question: Can I share or print the session?
faq.answer:
Share copies a link that restores the steps. Print puts the colored timeline on one landscape A4 page.

Example: load the interval example and choose Share. Opening that link shows the same 45:00 session.

A session that does not fit in a link should be exported as FIT, JSON, or DSL. Print and Share stay off until there is a step.

faq.answer:
The manual workout editor guide shows how to place the exported session on a Trainingload plan day.

Example: copy the DSL, open the guide, and paste it into Rules mode on the day you want.

Saving is a step you take in the app after you decide to keep the session.

answer.title: What is TSS?
answer.description: Training Stress Score combines workout duration and intensity relative to FTP into one load estimate.
answer.body:
TSS (Training Stress Score) combines how long you trained with how hard the session was relative to your FTP. In power-based cycling TSS, Normalized Power represents the cost of a variable ride, while Intensity Factor (IF) expresses that power as a fraction of FTP.

A score of 100 is the formula’s reference point for one hour at FTP. The same total can also come from a longer, easier ride or a shorter, harder effort, so TSS compares total load—not workout purpose, recovery time, or training quality.
answer.formula: IF = NP ÷ FTP; TSS = duration (hours) × IF² × 100
answer.example: Example: 90 minutes at 200 W NP with a 250 W FTP gives IF 0.80 and 96 TSS.
answer.npNote: Use Normalized Power when it is available. Average power can estimate a steady ride, but it does not reproduce how NP weights surges, climbs, and coasting.
answer.equivalents: This calculator returns power-based cycling TSS. rTSS, sTSS, and hrTSS use different inputs and models, so the scores are not interchangeable.

faq.question: How is TSS calculated?
faq.answer:
Power-based TSS = hours × (NP ÷ FTP)² × 100, where IF = NP ÷ FTP. A one-hour ride with NP equal to FTP calculates to 100 TSS.

For example, 1.5 hours at 200 W NP with a 250 W FTP gives an IF of 0.80 and 96 TSS. Duration has a linear effect; intensity factor has a squared effect.

faq.question: Can I use average power if I do not have NP?
faq.answer:
Yes. Select average power to estimate the result. The report keeps that source visible instead of treating it as NP.

The values may be close during steady riding. Intervals, hills and repeated surges can make average power understate the load. Keep the input source consistent when comparing activities.

faq.question: Does a higher TSS mean better training?
faq.answer:
TSS describes load, not session quality or progress. A higher score can come from more time, more intensity relative to FTP, or both.

Different workouts can produce the same TSS. Interpret it with your goals, recent load and recovery rather than using one target for everyone.

faq.question: Can this calculate heart-rate or running TSS?
faq.answer:
This calculator uses power-based TSS and needs duration, power and FTP. Heart-rate and running-pace load methods use different inputs and calculations.

Do not enter heart rate in the power field or assume scores from different methods are interchangeable.

faq.question: Why is my result unusually high?
faq.answer:
Check the duration units, power type and FTP. An FTP set too low increases IF and then magnifies TSS through the squared term. Mixing whole-activity duration with power from a shorter segment can also distort it.

Make sure power and duration describe the same part of the activity before interpreting the result.

faq.question: Can I save the result or explore daily load?
faq.answer:
Share copies a link containing your inputs. Opening it restores the power type and result. Print produces a color report.

To see how several days of load affect CTL, ATL and TSB, continue to the training load calculator and enter each day’s total.

faq.question: What does 100 TSS mean?
faq.answer:
For power-based cycling TSS, 100 is the reference score for one hour with Normalized Power equal to FTP. It is a mathematical anchor, not a daily target.

A longer ride below FTP can also total 100 TSS. That does not make it the same workout or imply the same recovery need.

faq.question: What is a good TSS score?
faq.answer:
There is no universal good score. A suitable load depends on your recent training, goals, fitness, and recovery. Compare the result with similar sessions and with your own weekly trend.

Use TSS to describe load, then keep duration, intensity distribution, terrain, heat, sleep, and perceived effort in the decision.

faq.question: How much TSS should I do per week?
faq.answer:
A weekly number without your history is not a useful prescription. Start from the load you have been completing consistently and watch how CTL, ATL, TSB, performance, and recovery respond.

Large jumps can be caused by a training change or by stale thresholds and mismatched data, so check the inputs before changing the plan.

formula.description: This CTL ATL TSB calculator updates each day in sequence. CTL responds gradually, ATL reacts faster, and their difference gives this page’s TSB.
formula.caption: One day of 100 TSS from CTL 50 and ATL 50
formula.note: In this example, CTL and ATL start equal, so ATL increases six times as much. Calculations retain full precision; this table shows two decimals and the report shows one.

faq.question: What can I use this calculator for?
faq.answer:
Enter starting CTL and ATL plus 7–14 consecutive days of TSS to explore how your load develops. Use completed sessions to review a period, or planned loads to compare possible schedules.

Each day feeds into the next. Include rest days as 0 rather than skipping them; changing one day affects that day and every later result.

faq.question: How does one training day change CTL and ATL?
faq.answer:
Starting from CTL 50 and ATL 50, a day with 100 TSS gives CTL = 50 + (100 − 50) / 42 = 51.19 and ATL = 50 + (100 − 50) / 7 = 57.14. Same-day TSB is −5.95.

Here the starting values are equal, so ATL increases six times as much. The 42- and 7-day constants control how quickly past load fades; they are not simple averages limited to those days.

faq.question: What happens on a rest day?
faq.answer:
Rest means 0 TSS, but previous training still fades over time. Starting at CTL 60 and ATL 80, one rest day gives CTL 58.57, ATL 68.57, and TSB −10.00.

ATL falls faster in this example, narrowing the gap. A small CTL drop reflects lower recent load in the model; it does not prove that a day off reduced your actual fitness.

faq.question: Is a higher TSB always better?
faq.answer:
This CTL ATL TSB calculator uses updated, same-day CTL minus ATL. A negative value means recent load exceeds the longer-term level; a positive value means recent load is lower. Neither sign alone establishes recovery or performance.

The −10 and +10 display boundaries are reading aids, not personal targets. Time off can also produce a large positive value, so consider your training phase and how you feel.

faq.question: Why do my numbers differ from another platform?
faq.answer:
Compare starting values, daily loads, and dates first. Platforms can use different load sources, decay formulas, or TSB date conventions.

This page updates by 1/42 and 1/7 and reports the same-day difference. TrainingPeaks Form uses the previous day’s CTL and ATL. Trainingload.ai’s full chart uses exponential decay, so results need not match exactly.

faq.question: Can I calculate without knowing my starting CTL and ATL?
faq.answer:
Yes. Keep the example to explore how training and rest change the curves. If you have historical readings, use values from before the first day you enter.

Starting at zero assumes no accumulated load. If you have been training, this understates your initial level. Consistent subsequent records gradually reduce the influence of the initial estimate.

faq.question: Can this help me plan a taper?
faq.answer:
You can compare planned daily loads and see how CTL, ATL, and TSB respond. There is no universal race-day TSB target.

Your sport, training history, event duration, and actual recovery also matter. Comparing with your own successful preparations is more useful than chasing a fixed score.

faq.question: Where does daily TSS come from? Can I upload a file?
faq.answer:
Use TSS from your training platform and add sessions completed on the same day. Keep the load source and threshold settings consistent where possible.

This page takes daily numbers and does not parse activity files. Estimate a session with the TSS calculator, or sync and import activities in Trainingload.ai for ongoing tracking.

faq.question: Can I save or share the report?
faq.answer:
Print the report or share a link containing your starting CTL, ATL, and daily TSS. Opening that link restores the same inputs and results.

Calculation happens in your browser and does not update your athlete profile. Shared links expose the inputs they contain, so share only data you want others to see.

answer.title: How this race time predictor works
answer.description: Daniels VDOT uses one race result to estimate equivalent performances at other distances.
answer.body: A 50:00 10K gives a VDOT of 40.0, equivalent to a 24:06 5K, a 1:50:54 half marathon and a 3:49:37 marathon. Your original result stays unchanged in the table; the other times are calculated at the same VDOT.
answer.formula:
VO2(v) = -4.6 + 0.182258 v + 0.000104 v²
%VO2max(t) = 0.8 + 0.1894393 e^(−0.012778 t) + 0.2989558 e^(−0.1932605 t)
VDOT = VO2(v) / %VO2max(t)
Round the starting VDOT to one decimal place, then solve for t at the target distance using that same VDOT.
v is speed in m/min; t is time in minutes. This calculator supports VDOT 20–85.
answer.limits: Riegel uses a different approach: T2 = T1 × (D2/D1)^1.06. A 25:00 5K gives a VDOT of 38.3, equivalent to a 51:54 10K and a 3:57:58 marathon. Riegel gives 52:07 and 3:59:47 for the same result. Neither calculation accounts for your effort level, preparation, weather or hills.

faq.question: Why does my predicted marathon time look too fast?
faq.answer:
Daniels VDOT assumes you are equally well prepared for each distance. Your 5K or 10K result may show good speed without showing whether you can sustain the equivalent marathon pace.

For example, a 50:00 10K gives a VDOT of 40.0 and a marathon equivalent of 3:49:37. A 25:00 5K gives a VDOT of 38.3 and a marathon equivalent of 3:57:58.

Long-run fitness, fueling and heat are not part of the calculation. Check those factors before choosing your race-day pace.

faq.question: How does this differ from Riegel's formula?
faq.answer:
The usual Riegel formula is T2 = T1 × (D2/D1)^1.06. Daniels VDOT instead models how the proportion of VO2max a runner can sustain changes with duration.

For a 25:00 5K, Riegel gives a 52:07 10K and a 3:59:47 marathon. Daniels VDOT gives 51:54 and 3:57:58.

The results table uses Daniels VDOT. Riegel is included here to explain why other calculators may give different times.

faq.question: Does the prediction account for weather or the course?
faq.answer:
No. This calculation uses distance and time only, without adjusting for temperature, wind, altitude or hills.

A 50:00 10K gives the same 3:49:37 marathon equivalent whether you ran it on a cool, flat course or a hot, hilly one. When your next race has different conditions, compare the estimate with performances on similar courses before choosing a goal.

faq.question: Can I use a training run instead of a race?
faq.answer:
Yes. You can use the whole run or a continuous segment between 1500 m and marathon distance from a GPX, FIT or TCX file.

Keep the effort in mind: an easy 10K generally gives a lower VDOT than a raced 10K at the same fitness level. The calculator uses the pace you actually ran and does not estimate how much faster you could have gone.

A lower result from an easy run does not, by itself, mean you have lost fitness.

faq.question: Will my activity file be uploaded?
faq.answer:
No. GPX, FIT and TCX files are read in your browser and stay on this device.

A usable segment needs continuous distance data. Segments with a recording gap over 10 seconds or a backward jump in distance are excluded. If no suitable segment between 1500 m and marathon distance is available, the calculator leaves the finish times blank.

faq.question: How does this differ from the VDOT and pace calculators?
faq.answer:
Use this page to compare equivalent finish times across race distances, with pace per kilometer and mile.

The VDOT calculator also gives Easy, Marathon, Threshold, Interval and Repetition training paces. The running pace calculator converts a chosen time and distance into a pace and even splits. Choose the tool that matches your next step.

faq.question: How should I train toward the predicted time?
faq.answer:
Start by checking whether the equivalent time fits your preparation. For example, a 50:00 10K gives a marathon equivalent of 3:49:37, about 5:27/km, but that does not tell you whether your marathon endurance is ready.

Once you have chosen a goal, use a 10K, half marathon or marathon plan to organize your training. Use the pace calculator to plan splits, and make room for long runs, fueling practice and recovery.

faq.question: Can I save or share my results?
faq.answer:
Share opens your device's sharing options or copies a link that restores the inputs. Print formats the results as a single landscape page.

This page does not save the result to your account. You can keep the link or printout, then open Trainingload.ai to plan your training around the goal you choose.

faq.question: Which race distance is most useful for a marathon prediction?
faq.answer:
If your results are equally recent and reflect comparable effort, a half marathon is closer to the target distance than a 5K or 10K. Shorter races are still useful, but speed over a short distance alone does not show marathon endurance.

Compare the estimates with your long runs, training consistency, fueling and target course before settling on a goal.

faq.question: Why is my Garmin race prediction different?
faq.answer:
This calculator uses one distance and finish time to calculate Daniels VDOT equivalents. Garmin also uses VO2max estimates and training history. Supported race-specific features may consider information about the event as well.

With different inputs, the predictions can differ. Compare both with your recent races and preparation rather than assuming one is always right.

definition.title: What is a race time predictor?
definition.body: A race time predictor uses a result you have already run to estimate your time at another distance. This calculator uses Daniels VDOT to compare equivalent 5K, 10K, half marathon and marathon performances. Use it as a guide when setting a goal, with your preparation for the target distance in mind.

accuracy.title: How accurate are race time predictions?
accuracy.body: A formula can compare performances, but it cannot account for everything that happens in a race. Read the estimate alongside your training and recent results before choosing a target.
checks: Use a recent race or sustained time trial that reflects your current fitness. An easy run shows your pace on that day, not necessarily your racing ability.
Compare similar courses and conditions. Heat, wind, elevation and trail terrain are not adjusted for here.
For longer races, consider your endurance and fueling practice. If recent results give different estimates, look at why rather than choosing only the fastest.
accuracy.research: A study of recreational runners found that Riegel could predict marathon times that were too fast. It highlights the importance of the model's assumptions, but does not tell us the error margin for this Daniels calculator.

cycling-training-plan.faqSubtitle: Gran fondo, century, FTP, TSS, and how this hub differs from an official running template.
faq: Is this an official Trainingload cycling training plan template?

No. Official week×day templates today cover running 5K, 10K, half marathon, and marathon. This page is a cycling training plan hub: phases, load method, and CTAs into the app. It does not export a fake power calendar.
How long should a cycling training plan be?
Twelve to sixteen weeks is a practical framework for a gran fondo or century if you already ride 60–90 minutes. Shorter blocks work for maintenance; longer base helps if endurance is thin.
Can I use this for a gran fondo or a century ride?
Yes. Those are modifiers on the same cycling training plan intent: build aerobic endurance, add some threshold, peak with event-specific rides, then taper. The app plan is what you actually follow.
Do I need FTP before I start?
FTP or CP makes TSS and zones honest. If you do not have one, estimate from an activity file, then update the plan when the number changes.
How do CTL, ATL, and TSB change the plan?
They show whether you are building, fatigued, or fresh. A static PDF cannot read them. Trainingload uses them when the AI cycling coach drafts the next adjustment.
Indoor trainer or outdoor—does the plan change?
The stimulus still has to match the week. Indoor sessions are easier to control; outdoor group rides often produce more TSS than planned. Log both and adjust.
How is this different from TrainerRoad or a PDF plan?
Those products may ship dense bike workouts. Trainingload’s difference is multi-sport load, a live plan, and confirmable AI changes after completed rides—not a silent rewrite of tomorrow’s intervals.
Where do I create the actual calendar?
In the Trainingload app. This URL explains the cycling training plan method. Plan creation, the workout editor, and AI confirmation happen in the product.

faq: Is there an official IRONMAN 70.3 training plan in Trainingload?
No. Official templates are running-only. This 70.3 training plan URL is a multi-sport hub: phases, load, eligibility, and CTAs to create the plan in-app.
What is a 70.3, a half Ironman, and a 113?

They name the same distance family: 1.9 km swim, 90 km bike, 21.1 km run (about 113 km total). Searchers use IRONMAN 70.3 training plan, 70.3 training plan, and 113 interchangeably; this page covers that intent.
How many weeks should a 70.3 training plan be?
Twelve to sixteen weeks is the framework if you already train all three sports. Add base weeks if the swim or bike is the limiter; do not compress peak bricks into an unprepared body.
How do I balance swim, bike, and run load?

Read combined CTL/ATL/TSB. The bike usually produces the most measurable TSS; the run creates musculoskeletal cost; the swim can still ruin freshness. Cut filler before cutting the key session in the weakest sport.
Do I need brick sessions?
Yes as a theme in build and peak: bike then run to rehearse stiffness and fueling. This page does not invent a brick workout library pretending to be an official template.
Is this a couch-to-70.3 plan?
No. Eligibility assumes you can already complete each sport. Start with running plans, a cycling training plan hub, and swim volume before stacking a 70.3 calendar.
How is this different from a PDF 70.3 plan?
A PDF cannot see completed files or training load. Trainingload drafts confirmable adjustments when one sport overreaches, instead of leaving Monday’s intervals untouched.
Can I reuse the official half marathon template for the run?
For a first 21.1 km, the free half marathon finish schedule is a legitimate run-leg starting point. It is still not a full 70.3 template; bike and swim must live on the same calendar.

faq: Is this an official Trainingload olympic triathlon training plan template?

No. Official week×day templates today cover running 5K, 10K, half marathon, and marathon. This page is an olympic triathlon training plan hub: phases, weekly structure, and load—not a fabricated day-by-day product calendar.
What distances does an olympic distance triathlon training plan cover?
Standard Olympic distance is 1.5 km swim, 40 km bike, and 10 km run. Sprint is shorter; IRONMAN 70.3 is longer (1.9 / 90 / 21.1). Use the 70.3 hub when that is the event.
How many hours per week for an olympic triathlon training plan?

Many intermediates sit around six to ten sessions and roughly 6–12 hours, depending on swim skill and bike endurance. Hours are a starting constraint, not a badge. Let CTL rise without keeping ATL slammed.
Where do bricks belong in the week?
Usually once in build and peak, after a quality or endurance bike. Read the brick workout hub. Do not stack a VO2 run the next morning by default.
What is CSS in an olympic triathlon training plan?

Critical swim speed (CSS) is a field-test swim threshold pace, analogous to bike FTP. Use 400 m and 200 m time trials as planning language. This site does not ship a CSS calculator; FTP and lactate-threshold tools cover the bike/run analogs.
Can AI write the whole Olympic calendar for me?

The product can help you create a triathlon plan and then draft adjustments from completed work and training load. It does not silently replace a coach, and this hub does not pretend a JSON template already exists.
How is this different from a 70.3 training plan?
Olympic emphasizes a faster 10 km and a shorter bike. 70.3 needs more durability and a half-marathon run. Same load loop; different duration and fueling cost.

metadata.title: Brick Workout: Bike-to-Run Training for Triathlon
metadata.description: What a brick workout is, bike-to-run formats, and how brick training hits CTL, ATL, and TSB. Educational triathlon guidance, then draft it in the editor.

openGraph.title: Brick Workout and Brick Training
openGraph.description: Learn triathlon brick sessions, load cost, and how to place them in a plan.

jsonLd.name: Brick Workout Guide
jsonLd.description: Educational hub for triathlon brick workouts: bike-to-run formats, load and fatigue notes, and product CTAs into plan hubs and the workout editor.

page.title: Brick Workouts
page.subtitle: Understand how to link two sports in one session, choose the purpose and review the load.

purpose.title: Choose a purpose
purpose.body: Decide whether you are practising transitions, pacing, nutrition or equipment. Let that purpose shape the session.

format.title: Link two disciplines
format.body: Bike-to-run is a common format. Swim-to-bike may also fit your event. Include the transition in your plan.

load.title: Review both parts together
load.body: Consider duration, intensity and how both parts felt before planning the next session.

answer.title: What is a brick workout?
answer.description: Two disciplines linked by a short transition.
answer.body: A brick workout is commonly used in triathlon training. Bike-to-run is the best-known format: it helps you practise changing movement patterns, equipment, fueling and pace.
answer.why: The link between disciplines is the focus. Fatigue from the ride can affect how the run feels, so review the whole session rather than judging the run by pace alone.

formats.title: Common brick formats
formats.description: Use these to choose a purpose. Duration and intensity depend on your experience and wider training plan.

cards.title: Endurance ride → easy run
cards.body: Follow a familiar riding effort with a short, controlled run. Focus on finding your rhythm after the transition.

cards.title: Key ride → short run
cards.body: Let the ride carry the main training work, and use the run to practise the transition. Both parts do not need to be hard.

cards.title: Short transition practice
cards.body: Use short bike-to-run segments to rehearse equipment changes and settling into your running rhythm.

cards.title: Race routine practice
cards.body: Rehearse equipment, fueling and pacing in event order. Include the total load and recovery in your plan.

load.title: Reviewing the total load
load.description: Two activity files can still represent one continuous session.
items: Include both disciplines in your review. Load methods can differ by sport, so keep comparisons consistent.
Record how the transition felt. The same running pace may bring a different heart rate and effort after cycling.
CTL, ATL and TSB describe load patterns. They do not independently determine readiness for another hard session.
Use sleep, recovery, goals and what you actually completed to adjust the next session.

faq.question: How is a brick different from two separate workouts?
faq.answer:
The transition is the defining feature. A brick links disciplines in one session to practise changing movement patterns and pace. With a long break and substantial recovery between them, they are closer to two separate workouts.

Either arrangement can be useful; choose it for the purpose of that session.

faq.question: Should every ride finish with a run?
faq.answer:
No. A brick serves transition practice and event preparation; it is not a required ending to every ride.

Frequency depends on experience, training phase and recovery. If it makes your next important session difficult to complete, reconsider its length or frequency.

faq.question: How long and fast should the run be?
faq.answer:
Start with the purpose. Transition practice can focus on a short, controlled run; a race rehearsal needs to reflect the event and the training you have already built.

Do not judge intensity from a stand-alone running pace alone. Record heart rate, movement quality and perceived effort after the transition.

faq.question: Can a brick replace a long run?
faq.answer:
Their purposes differ. A brick emphasizes the link between disciplines, while a separate run gives more room for focused run training.

Consider the whole week, your priorities and recovery. Total bike-plus-run duration is not automatically equivalent to the same duration of running.

faq.question: How can I plan and record one?
faq.answer:
Use the workout editor to outline each discipline’s warm-up, main work and cool-down, and retain the completed cycling and running records.

In Trainingload.ai, review the plan, activities and load together before adjusting what comes next.

faq.question: Are these formats a personal training plan?
faq.answer:
They explain different purposes and formats. They do not account for your history, event date or current recovery.

A usable plan still needs duration, intensity and transition details, with adjustments based on how you respond.

methods.title: Methods and formulas
methods.description: Four ways to estimate one aerobic range. Use the benchmark you trust most.
methods.caption: Zone 2 methods and percent bands

rows.use: You have a tested max HR or an observed peak from a hard effort.
You know both max HR and resting HR and want a range adjusted for heart-rate reserve.
You have a threshold heart rate from a steady hard effort. A 30-minute test is one protocol.
Age is the only number available. A later measured max HR can replace it.

methods.note: Example: max HR 190 → 114–132 bpm. Max HR 190 with resting HR 50 → 134–147 bpm by Karvonen. LTHR 170 → 138–152 bpm. Age 40 with Tanaka → 108–125 bpm.

faq.question: How do I figure out my Zone 2 heart rate?
faq.answer:
Choose the benchmark you know best. Max HR uses 60–70%. Karvonen uses 60–70% of heart-rate reserve and needs both max HR and resting HR. Friel uses 81–89% of LTHR. If age is all you know, the calculator estimates HRmax first.

Use the result as a starting point, then check that breathing stays steady and full sentences remain comfortable.

faq.question: What percentage is Zone 2 heart rate?
faq.answer:
In the five-zone max-HR model, Zone 2 is 60–70% of max HR. Karvonen applies the same 60–70% to heart-rate reserve and adds resting HR. Friel cycling Zone 2 is 81–89% of LTHR.

These percentages describe different models, so the bpm ranges are not expected to match exactly.

faq.question: Can a normal workout stand in for a max test?
faq.answer:
Yes, when the workout gives you a usable max HR or LTHR. An observed peak from a hard effort can stand in for max HR, and a steady hard section can stand in for LTHR. The 30-minute test is one LTHR protocol, not the only evidence that counts.

An easy day that never got hard will sit below a true max or threshold. That changes how representative the estimate is. Compare it with the number you already train from and decide whether to adopt it.

faq.question: Why does this differ from my watch?
faq.answer:
Watches may use percent of max HR, heart-rate reserve, LTHR, or a proprietary table, and they may round boundaries differently. This page shows the selected method beside the result.

Compare the model and its anchor before comparing bpm. Keep one method consistent long enough to make training sessions comparable.

faq.question: How do I train with this range?
faq.answer:
Use this bpm range as a guide on easy endurance days. With a max HR of 190, the max-HR method gives 114–132 bpm. Twenty minutes is still useful; when you are well recovered, 30–60 minutes adds more aerobic volume.

You should still be able to speak comfortably in full sentences. Slow down if talking becomes difficult, even when your watch says you are still in range.

faq.question: Is 75% of max heart rate still Zone 2?
faq.answer:
Not in the 60–70% max-HR model. 75% of 190 is about 143 bpm, above the 132 bpm ceiling. Some LTHR or heart-rate-reserve charts give a similar effort a different zone number.

If conversation breaks up, treat the effort as harder than Zone 2.

faq.question: Can I save or share the result?
faq.answer:
Print the scorecard or share a link that keeps the method and the number you entered. The page does not write the range into your account.

Saving it in custom heart-rate zones is a separate step you start in the app. An example result is labeled so you can replace it before sharing.

faq.answer:

definition.title: What is Zone 2 heart rate?
definition.answer: Zone 2 heart rate is a sustainable aerobic intensity commonly defined as 60–70% of maximum heart rate, 60–70% of heart-rate reserve, or 81–89% of LTHR in the Friel cycling model.
definition.detail: Those formulas can produce different bpm ranges because they use different anchors. Treat the number as a starting point and check it against steady breathing and the ability to speak in full sentences.

ageTable.title: Zone 2 heart rate by age
ageTable.body: These reference ranges use the Tanaka estimate, 208 − 0.7 × age, followed by 60–70% of estimated max HR.
ageTable.caption: Zone 2 heart rate ranges by age using the Tanaka formula
ageTable.note: Age formulas describe population averages. A measured max HR, resting HR, or reliable LTHR can give you a more individual starting point.

feel.title: How should Zone 2 feel?
feel.body: Use breathing and perceived effort to check the calculated range during real training.

cards.title: Talk test
cards.body: You should be able to speak in full sentences without gasping. Short, broken phrases usually mean the effort has moved above an easy aerobic intensity.

cards.title: Heart-rate drift
cards.body: Heart rate can rise during a steady session as heat, dehydration, fatigue, hills, or duration accumulate. Slow down when the same pace no longer feels easy.

cards.title: Watch differences
cards.body: Watches may use percent of max HR, heart-rate reserve, or LTHR and may round boundaries differently. Compare the underlying model before comparing the bpm.

handoff.title: Need all of your heart-rate zones?

method.title: Method & formula
method.description: Plot both swims by distance and time. The slope of the line between them is this tool’s CSS estimate.
method.caption: Critical swim speed formula

rows.bestFor: Two different distances, in matching units
rows.limit: The longer swim must take longer; 400 / 200 is common, not mandatory

rows.bestFor: Turn speed into a useful training pace
rows.limit: m/s gives pace per 100 m; yd/s gives pace per 100 yd

details.title: Two-point model: distance and time differences
details.method: Order the swims by distance. D2 and T2 are the longer swim; D1 and T1 are the shorter. Divide the difference in distance by the difference in time.
details.basis: This is a linear distance–time model. 400 m in 360 s and 200 m in 160 s give a slope of 1.00 m/s.
details.limits: Two points cannot test goodness of fit. Different strokes, effort levels, or timing conventions may produce a number that poorly represents threshold ability.

details.title: Metres, yards, and pace
details.method: One yard is 0.9144 metres. Switching units converts distance and pace while preserving time. Speed is always displayed in m/s.
details.basis: For example, 1:40 /100 m converts to about 1:31 /100 yd: two ways of expressing the same speed.
details.limits: Unit conversion does not adjust for turns in 25 m versus 50 m pools, current, stroke, or equipment.

details.title: Choose existing swims or a dedicated test
details.method: Existing records work too. Prefer continuous swims with the same stroke and similar conditions, excluding rest. A recovered, well-paced 400 / 200 time trial can give a better view of your current limits.
details.basis: Wakayoshi and colleagues studied critical velocity with distance–time models. The 400 / 200 pair is a practical testing method, not the only input allowed by the formula.
details.limits: Effort affects how representative an estimate is, not whether it can be calculated. Nearly equal distances amplify timing errors; mixing sprints with easy long swims also needs care when interpreting the result.

zones.title: Turn CSS into training paces
zones.description: These references add or subtract seconds from CSS pace per 100 m. They are not five continuous physiological zones. Set distance, rest, and effort alongside pace.
zones.caption: Training pace reference offsets

meanings.easy: Recovery, easy swimming, and technique; go slower if needed
meanings.aerobic: Steady swimming with controlled breathing and technique
meanings.threshold: A reference for sustained swims or sets
meanings.speed: Shorter repeats while maintaining stroke quality

zones.example: At 1:40 /100 m CSS: easy 1:48–1:52, steady aerobic 1:44–1:47, CSS pace 1:40, faster repeats 1:36–1:38, short repeats 1:32–1:35. The scorecard converts these paces when you select yards.
zones.source: These fixed offsets are training references used by this tool, not zone boundaries established by the Wakayoshi study.

faq.question: What is CSS? Is it the same as lactate threshold?
faq.answer:
Critical Swim Speed is an estimate from a distance–time model. This calculator fits a line through two swims of different distances, uses its slope as speed, and expresses the result as pace per 100 metres or yards. It can help set a starting pace for training.

It is not a laboratory lactate measurement or a promise that you can sustain that speed indefinitely. Its usefulness depends on effort, stroke, conditions, and how well the pace matches your actual swimming.

faq.question: How do two swims produce a 1:40 pace?
faq.answer:
For 400 m in 6:00 (360 seconds) and 200 m in 2:40 (160 seconds), the distance difference is 200 m and the time difference is 200 seconds. CSS is 200 ÷ 200 = 1.00 m/s. That means 100 seconds per 100 m, or 1:40.

Those differences are calculated between two swims. They do not mean you actually swam a separate 200 m segment in 3:20. The chart shows the relationship used by the model.

faq.question: Do I need a new all-out 200 / 400 test?
faq.answer:
No. Start with two existing swims of different distances. The basic requirements are valid positive distances and times, with more time for the longer swim. Ordinary training records can produce an estimate.

If both swims were comfortable, the result describes those performances and may not represent your current limits. A dedicated test improves comparability, but is not a prerequisite for calculation. Use the estimate as a starting point and check it against training.

faq.question: Can I use distances other than 200 and 400?
faq.answer:
Yes. Different distances and a longer time for the longer swim satisfy the two-point formula. Input order does not matter. The 400 / 200 metre or yard pair is a common, repeatable option.

Prefer the same stroke and similar conditions. Nearly equal distances magnify small timing errors; pairing a short sprint with a long easy swim also changes what the result represents. Being calculable and being representative are separate questions.

faq.question: Which swim files are supported?
faq.answer:
FIT, TCX, and GPX are supported, with up to two files of 20 MB each. One file containing two different-distance swims is enough; alternatively, choose one record from each of two activities. You choose the records after seeing their distances and times.

FIT rest markers can separate continuous swimming bouts; otherwise the tool reads laps or session summaries. TCX supplies laps and GPX supplies track segments. If a file has only one usable record, add another file or enter the second swim manually.

faq.question: Do rests, automatic laps, and GPS affect the estimate?
faq.answer:
Yes. Rest included in a time changes the time difference. An automatic lap may simply be a device distance split, not a complete timed effort. Choose records that represent comparable continuous swims and check both timing conventions.

GPX uses elapsed track-segment time and may include stops. Open-water distances can also be affected by GPS error and current. A readable file does not make every record equally suitable. Use manual input when you know the correct distance and swimming time.

faq.question: Why does pace change when I switch metres and yards?
faq.answer:
Switching units converts the same records. One yard equals 0.9144 metres, so 1:40 /100 m is approximately 1:31 /100 yd. Distances and displayed pace change; times and speed in m/s stay the same.

For a 400 yd and 200 yd test, select yards before entering the actual distances. Different pool lengths change the number of turns. This is a unit conversion, not a performance prediction for another pool.

faq.question: How should I use the pace references?
faq.answer:
They add or subtract fixed seconds from CSS pace per 100 m. With 1:40 CSS, the easy reference is 1:48–1:52 and faster repeats are 1:36–1:38. Positive offsets are slower; negative offsets are faster.

These references do not cover every pace or define measured physiological zones. Easy swimming can be slower. Combine pace with repetition distance, rest, technique, and how you feel. Begin with sets you can complete consistently and adjust from there.

faq.question: Does an unusual-pace notice invalidate my result?
faq.answer:
No. This tool prompts you to check paces faster than 0:55 or slower than 3:00 per 100 m, but still calculates the result. Those limits are not a validity boundary for every stroke or ability level.

Check units, distances, seconds, and rest first, then judge the estimate against your own swimming. Calculation is blocked only when its mathematical inputs fail, such as equal distances, invalid times, or a longer swim that does not take longer.

faq.question: When should I update CSS, and can I mix strokes?
faq.answer:
Recalculate when you have useful comparable records or when sessions become noticeably easier or harder. You do not need frequent maximal tests just to update a number. Similar strokes, pools, and timing conventions make changes easier to interpret.

Freestyle versus breaststroke, fins versus no fins, and short-course versus long-course swims may give different results. Compare like with like and use several workouts, rather than treating one tired day as a loss of ability.

faq.question: Does sharing or printing save CSS to my account?
faq.answer:
Printing creates a colour landscape scorecard. Sharing opens your device share sheet or copies a link containing the two distances, times, and units, so someone else can reproduce the estimate. Files stay in your browser; the link contains no original file, route, or name.

This page does not automatically change account thresholds or plans. In the app, use your records to decide what to set and how to train. Choose whom to share with, since the link includes your calculation inputs.
